Tehran’s newspapers agree across factions that negotiating with the United States is legitimate, but are deeply divided over whether diplomacy can still prevent war, as Qatar said on Tuesday that both sides were reviewing its proposals.

Iranian protester was put through a mock hanging before his execution, source says. Amirhossein Maleki, a 20-year-old protester hanged in Isfahan on Tuesday, was blindfolded, given a noose and had a chair kicked from under him in a mock execution after he retracted a confession he said was extracted by torture, a source told Iran International.

Iran International's Negar Mojtahedi receives prestigious Canadian journalism award. Iran International journalist Negar Mojtahedi received the 2026 Bill Good Award at the 40th annual Webster Awards in Vancouver on Monday, in recognition of her reporting on war, state violence and human rights violations in Iran, often at great risk to her personal safety.

Iranians say they cannot afford emergency kits as fears of renewed war grow. Iranians responding to an Iran International appeal said they could not afford emergency supplies or had nowhere safe to go if wider war resumes with the United States and Israel, with others describing exhaustion after repeated rounds of fighting.

Internet disruptions hit Iran amid prospect of renewed US strikes. Internet users in Tehran and several other provinces reported outages and unstable connections Tuesday amid uncertainty over renewed US military action, after the New York Times reported that Washington could launch strikes on Iran as early as Wednesday.

US can't end Iran war with symbolic Pickaxe strike, state TV commentators say. Iranian commentators are questioning whether Donald Trump can end the conflict with a short military operation, arguing that the unresolved confrontation over Hormuz and the threat of economic retaliation could frustrate an attempt to strike Iran and declare victory.

Tehran students stage sit-in as dozens summoned in southeastern Iran. Iranian students face mounting security pressure, with sit-ins in Tehran after a doctoral student set himself on fire following repeated disciplinary summonses and reports of dozens summoned by intelligence authorities in the southeast.

Iran looks to China and Russia for leverage in US talks. Iran has turned to Beijing and Moscow for backing in talks with Washington over the Strait of Hormuz. Mediators are weighing whether China could help guarantee that Washington delivers on sanctions relief in return for Iranian nuclear concessions.

Trump says Iran war decision serves long-term US interests despite election setbacks. US President Donald Trump said his decision to launch the war against Iran remained in the long-term interests of the United States and the world, despite rising fuel prices and Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Iran's Araghchi regularly seeks talks amid efforts to avert renewed war, Germany says. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi regularly requests talks with his German counterpart as Berlin works with regional countries to prevent renewed US and Israeli attacks on Iran, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Wednesday.

Could Democrats' midterm victory accelerate Trump's Iran war?. Democrats' victory in both chambers of Congress could strengthen oversight of Donald Trump's war with Iran, but some analysts say the electoral setback may encourage the US president to intensify military operations before the new Congress takes office in January.

Iran executed at least 77 people in October, rights group says. Iran executed at least 77 people in October, bringing the total recorded this year to 691, including 36 protesters, Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) said on Tuesday.

Trump's Iran policy draws mixed reactions after Democrats' victory. The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections has drawn mixed reactions from Iran International's audience, with some criticizing Donald Trump's prolonged indecision over Iran and others maintaining that Democratic control of Congress will not prevent military action.

Iran can repair war damage, but can it revive its energy industry?. Iran may be able to repair much of its war-damaged energy infrastructure without new Western technology. Whether it can rebuild a modern, reliable energy industry is another question.

Iran sentences activist to death over X posts, lawyer says. A Revolutionary Court in Tehran has sentenced social media activist Amirhossein Mousavi to death on charges of "corruption on earth" over his activity on X, his lawyer said Wednesday.

Tehran's war debate turns to wider strikes and nuclear threats. The prospect of another war with Israel and the United States continues to dominate debate in Tehran despite a stinging electoral rebuke to President Donald Trump, driven in part by his military campaign against Iran.

Democrats demand end to Iran war after US midterm sweep. Democratic leaders vowed Wednesday to push for an end to the Iran war and tackle rising living costs after sweeping US midterm election victories handed their party control of both chambers of Congress.

Gold loses its shine as Iranians struggle to make ends meet. For years, Iranians have turned to gold to protect their savings from the relentless depreciation of the rial. Now, as war and soaring living costs deepen the economic crisis, some are selling those holdings to pay for everyday necessities.

Vance blames Iran war for election losses as Trump weighs next move against Tehran. US Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' sweeping midterm election defeats, including the loss of both chambers of Congress, as President Donald Trump weighed renewed military strikes against Tehran or a negotiated settlement to end the conflict.

Russia agreed to supply Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers - FT. Russia agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, revealing another dimension of Moscow's military cooperation with Tehran.

Iranian state TV broadcasts mock hanging of Trump live. Iranian state television broadcast live a mock hanging of US President Donald Trump as part of a pro-establishment campaign featuring public displays calling for his killing, following Republican losses in Tuesday's US midterm elections.

Inside the IRGC-linked corporate network controlling Iran’s internet. The companies that run Iran’s telecommunications are tied to the Revolutionary Guards through military-linked businesses, state foundations and technology contractors, an Iran International investigation has found, a system that lets the authorities decide who gets online.

Unpaid insurance bills push Iran's private hospitals into financial strain. Unpaid insurance reimbursements and rising medicine and equipment prices are draining private hospitals' finances, threatening their ability to maintain services and increasing costs for patients, hospital executives said in accounts published on Thursday.

Why social control remains central to Tehran's survival. Even as Iran grapples with war, economic crisis and the threat of renewed US and Israeli attacks, its security forces are breaking up Halloween celebrations, closing cafes and detaining people for gathering in public.

US condemns Iran protest executions, highlights families’ suffering. The US State Department on Thursday condemned Iran’s execution of three young men detained over January protests, highlighting their families’ suffering amid a broader campaign of executions that rights monitors say extends far beyond political cases.

Iran sentences two more protesters to death, rights group says. An Iranian court has sentenced two men arrested during January's anti-government protests to death, a rights group reported Thursday, adding to a growing number of protesters facing execution in the northeastern city of Mashhad.

Iran steps up diplomacy as Trump reels from midterm defeat. Iran stepped up diplomatic efforts on Thursday, submitting a new nuclear proposal to Washington, seeking Russian support and reaching out to regional powers a day after President Donald Trump's party suffered a sweeping defeat in the US midterm elections.

Iran hardliners warn against compromise after US election shakeup. Iranian hardliners are calling for continued pressure on Washington following the US midterm elections, arguing that the war has exacted a political price on Republicans but that Democratic gains offer little prospect of a change in US policy toward Tehran.

Trump's election defeat fuels debate in Tehran over US deal. President Donald Trump's sweeping midterm defeat has sparked a debate in Tehran over whether Iran should seize the opportunity to negotiate a deal with Washington or maintain pressure through its control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Turkey's Mecca pact ratification paves way for military support to Saudi Arabia. Turkey's approval of a defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan has paved the way for military support to Riyadh amid attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, though deploying Turkish troops would still require separate parliamentary approval.

Free prisoners first: Jalali's wife challenges Tehran's call for expats to return. The wife of imprisoned Swedish-Iranian researcher Ahmadreza Jalali has challenged Tehran's calls for expatriates to return home, urging authorities to first release those jailed after visiting Iran.

Iran strike remains possible as IDF awaits Washington’s next move - Ynet. An Israeli strike on Iran remains possible, but Israeli defense officials have detected no major US military buildup in the region, Ynet reported on Friday, citing unnamed defense officials.

One man’s road from Westminster to the machine that carries Iran’s story abroad. An Iran International investigation has uncovered financial records and professional ties that shed light on how Tehran’s influence operations extend beyond its state broadcasters into ostensibly independent media outlets around the world.

Iran threatened Belgium over Pahlavi’s Brussels speech, defense minister says. Belgium’s defense minister said on Friday that Tehran had warned his country of dire consequences if it allowed Reza Pahlavi, Iran’s exiled prince, to speak in Brussels, and that the event had gone ahead anyway.

Iran-linked ships go dark over Persian Gulf internet cables after threats - FT. Ships linked to Iran looped, loitered and went dark over undersea internet cables in the Gulf of Oman in the weeks after Tehran threatened the region’s digital infrastructure, the Financial Times reported on Friday. One of them had been boarded by US Marines in May.

Gas-rich Iran turns to Russia for an energy lifeline. Iran, home to the world's second-largest natural gas reserves, is turning to Russia for supplies as war damage and years of underinvestment threaten to deepen an energy crisis ahead of winter.

Khamenei sent security chief to Moscow to seek S-400 air defenses – report. Iran sent security chief Mohsen Rezaei to Moscow to request S-400 air defense systems in a personal letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to President Vladimir Putin, The Telegraph reported Friday, citing a senior Iranian official.

US urges Iranians to stay away from IRGC positions if tensions escalate. A US military official urged Iranian civilians to remain indoors and stay away from Revolutionary Guards positions if military tensions escalate, telling Iran International that the IRGC was placing weapons and command centers in residential areas.

Opportunity or trap? Vance's Iran war remarks divide Tehran. Iranian commentators are divided over JD Vance's remarks on the political costs of the war with Iran, with some seeing evidence of tensions within the Trump administration and others warning that he may be trying to lure Tehran into a disadvantageous deal.

Iran presses ahead with military, nuclear rebuilding despite economic woes. New satellite imagery suggests Iran is undertaking major construction near missile bases and repairing military installations damaged by months of US and Israeli airstrikes, according to an investigation by BBC Verify.

Tehran hails US economic pain as Iranians struggle to make ends meet. While Tehran celebrates Donald Trump's midterm defeat and the economic pain the Iran war has inflicted on Americans, soaring prices and stagnant wages are pushing ordinary Iranians deeper into a cost-of-living crisis at home.

Netanyahu's pre-election Iran operation was dropped after US was tipped off - Channel 12. Israel’s prime minister and his Mossad chief planned an operation against Iran on the eve of Israel's October 27 election, over the objections of other security chiefs, and dropped it after a mistake by an Israeli operative tipped off Washington, Channel 12 reported on Friday.

Iran hangs Baluch man over attack on police post in Sistan and Baluchestan. Iran executed Mohammad Aref Shahbakhsh on Saturday over an armed attack on a police post in Khash, in the southeastern province of Sistan and Baluchestan, the judiciary said, the latest hanging as fighting between Baluch militants and security forces spreads across the province.

Iran’s exiled prince accepts German Freedom Prize for Iranians as thousands rally. Iran’s exiled prince Reza Pahlavi accepted Germany’s Freedom Prize for the Iranian people in Frankfurt on Saturday, its first award to a nation rather than a person, and said he would hold it until he could hand it to them in Tehran, as tens of thousands rallied in the city.

Sidi Ould Tah, George Elombi, Samaila Zubairu… À l’AFIS, les architectes de la finance africaine donnent corps à la Nafad. À l’occasion de l’Africa Financial Summit (AFIS), les dirigeants de la Banque africaine de développement, d’Afreximbank et d’Africa Finance Corporation ont parlé d’une même voix pour un objectif commun : le financement des besoins de l’Afrique par l’Afrique.

RDC : Shabani répond à Katumbi et menace la C64 de poursuites si elle rencontre Kabila à Goma. Le vice-Premier ministre et ministre de l’Intérieur brandit le Code pénal contre les leaders de la coalition d’opposition C64, qui projettent de rencontrer Joseph Kabila à Goma. En exclusivité pour Jeune Afrique, il évoque de possibles poursuites judiciaires.

Côte d’Ivoire : Esca, Polytechnique, Travaux publics… Les puissants réseaux des grandes écoles. Ces établissements d’élite, tous situés à Yamoussoukro, constituent un vivier de futurs ministres, patrons ou hauts fonctionnaires. Leurs diplômés disposent de relais aussi bien au cœur du pouvoir que dans les entreprises. Des liens solides qui ouvrent les portes.

Cameroun : l’incendie de Metafrique Steel à Douala va-t-il devenir un scandale et une affaire judiciaire ?. Un incendie s’est déclaré le 2 novembre dans une usine métallurgique de Douala, faisant au moins quatre morts. Les autorités politiques se sont rendues sur place, mais les avocats des victimes mettent la pression. Coulisses.

Guerre de pouvoir à la tête de Tabital Pulaaku : la communauté peule face à ses divisions. Une crise sans précédent déchire Tabital Pulaaku International, dont la présidence est disputée entre le Nigérian Sanusi II, émir de Kano, et le Sierra-Léonais Amadou Djouldé Sow. Coulisses et révélations sur un bras de fer dans lequel la junte malienne joue un rôle clé.

TotalEnergies, Shell, BP… Pourquoi le raffinage ne séduit plus les majors en Afrique ?. Alors que l’offensive du milliardaire nigérian Aliko Dangote redonne des couleurs à l’activité de transformation de pétrole, les géants du secteur boudent cette filière sur le continent. Décryptage.

Bénin : face à Romuald Wadagni, Nourénou Atchadé, nouveau leader d’une opposition ostracisée. Consacré chef des Démocrates lors du congrès de Porto-Novo, Nourénou Atchadé hérite d’un parti en crise. Entre querelles judiciaires et traversée du désert politique et financière, récit d’une succession sous haute tension au Bénin.

Au Sahara, qui va occuper la zone tampon située à l’est du mur après le départ de la Minurso ?. Après trente-cinq ans de présence, la mission de l’ONU au Sahara prépare son départ. Au-delà de l’opération logistique, le retrait des Nations unies pourrait ouvrir la voie à un redéploiement des Forces armées royales à l’est du mur de défense marocain.

10 choses à savoir sur Sidy Cissé, le polytechnicien qui doit dynamiser la Caisse des dépôts et consignations de Côte d’Ivoire. Ayant fait ses armes au sein du ministère du Budget et de la primature, ce technocrate est habitué à gérer les grands projets et les dossiers de financement. Une expérience clé pour faire entrer la CDC-CI dans une nouvelle phase de son développement.

300 champions de la finance : les francophones prêtent, les Nigérians couvrent. Portées par les investissements dans les infrastructures et le BTP, les banques francophones prêtent massivement leur épargne. Un dynamisme qui tranche avec la pratique des groupes nigérians, freinés par de fortes contraintes réglementaires.

Pourquoi Fouzi Lekjaâ va démissionner de son poste de président de la Commission des finances de la CAF. Récemment nommé à la tête d’un super-ministère marocain de l’Économie, des Finances et de la Performance publique, Fouzi Lekjaâ occupe également plusieurs fonctions sportives, dont la présidence de la commission des finances de la CAF. Un poste qu’il va quitter prochainement, la charge de ses différentes fonctions – parmi lesquelles l’organisation du Mondial 2030 – devenant trop importante.

Attijariwafa bank : après le boom des infrastructures au Maroc, cap sur l’Afrique. Rentable et dominant, le premier groupe bancaire du Maroc vient de renouer avec les acquisitions. Un premier pas prudent alors que se profile l’échéance de 2030 et la fin d’un cycle d’investissements qui a dopé son bilan.

Au Sénégal, Bassirou Diomaye Faye parviendra-t-il à faire aboutir les négociations avec les rebelles casamançais ?. À Ziguinchor, la gendarmerie a évacué le siège historique du MFDC, rappelant la ligne rouge tracée par Dakar face aux indépendantistes. Malgré l’accalmie, le gouvernement peine à concrétiser les négociations de paix.

Côte d’Ivoire : un an plus tard, où en sont les enquêtes sur les violences électorales dans l’Ouest ?. Un an après l’élection présidentielle d’octobre 2025, les familles des victimes de Nahio inhument les morts des violences survenues en marge du scrutin. Malgré les enquêtes annoncées par la justice ivoirienne, le dossier reste au point mort.

En RDC, le virage américain de Félix Tshisekedi peut-il payer ?. Conclu en décembre 2025 en même temps que l’accord de paix, le partenariat stratégique entre la RDC et les États-Unis se met progressivement en place. Il pourrait, à terme, pâtir de l’absence d’avancées concrètes dans le conflit dans l’est du pays.

« Rien n’est joué » : malgré les doutes, Kinshasa veut croire en Juliana Lumumba, sa candidate pour l’OIF. Le camp congolais affiche sa confiance pour la conquête du secrétariat général de l’Organisation internationale de la francophonie mi-novembre. Mais, en off, plusieurs sources dressent un bilan plus nuancé de la campagne : si la RDC suscite de la sympathie, la candidate peine à convaincre.

Cameroun : Sylvestre Ngouchinghe, le roi du poisson face au poison du soupçon. Longtemps considéré comme l’un des hommes d’affaires les mieux installés dans les réseaux du pouvoir, le patron de Congelcam traverse une période difficile. Derrière les déboires de son empire, l’ombre d’un soupçon politique, né au lendemain de la présidentielle de 2018.

Dette africaine : le grand retour sur les marchés mais à quel prix ?. Les États subsahariens émettent de nouveau massivement sur les marchés internationaux. Mais, face à des coupons en hausse et des maturités raccourcies, la Banque mondiale met en garde contre un accès aux capitaux qui s’est dégradé.

Au Maroc, une étude souligne le trop faible accès des femmes au monde du travail. Selon une récente étude, plus de quatre Marocaines sur cinq sont écartées du marché du travail, et la proportion ne s’améliore pas. Alors que le gouvernement est, pour la première fois, dirigé par une femme, les chercheurs soulignent que la question de la place assignée aux femmes dans la famille doit être posée.

Tony Elumelu : « Nous devons industrialiser l’Afrique, personne d’autre que nous ne le fera ». Futur président de Seplat Energy, Tony Elumelu renforce son emprise sur le secteur énergétique nigérian. Dans cet entretien, il explique comment la finance nationale fait émerger une nouvelle économie industrielle.

Assimi Goïta en Russie : le président malien et l’escort girl de Vladimir Poutine. Le chef de la junte au pouvoir à Bamako a effectué une visite à Moscou, pour le sommet Russie-Afrique des 28 et 29 octobre. L’occasion d’échanges diplomatiques et sécuritaires, mais aussi d’un exercice de tir filmé puis retransmis à la télévision nationale malienne. Sur les images, une mystérieuse assistante a attiré l’attention.

Pays bénéficiaires vs pays donateurs : qui profite vraiment de l’aide publique au développement ?. Véritable tendance de fond aux États-Unis, en France ou au Japon, la baisse des crédits alloués à l’aide publique au développement comporte un paradoxe : elle peut jouer en défaveur des pays donateurs, qui y perdent certaines contreparties économiques et géopolitiques. Tel est le résultat, sans appel, d’une étude menée par trois chercheurs.

De Kinshasa à Lubumbashi, comment la RDC tente de moderniser ses aéroports. Avec les chantiers de rénovation, déjà bien avancés, des terminaux de Ndjili et de la Luano, le gouvernement congolais va enfin pouvoir remettre les plus grands hubs aériens du pays aux standards internationaux.

Lutte contre l’orpaillage illégal en Guinée : pourquoi l’offensive de Mamadi Doumbouya tend les relations avec l’AES. Conakry a ordonné l’interdiction de l’orpaillage clandestin à Siguiri et a expulsé des centaines d’orpailleurs ouest-africains. Une offensive sécuritaire et environnementale qui provoque des tensions diplomatiques avec le Mali et le Burkina Faso.

Guerres d’influences au Sahel : comment le nouvel accord Tiani-Haftar redistribue les cartes entre Alger et Abou Dhabi. Le Niger et les autorités de Benghazi ont scellé un pacte de non-agression pour éviter un conflit par procuration. Derrière cette réconciliation, les Émirats arabes unis et l’Algerie se livrent une lutte d’influence directe dans le Fezzan.

OIF : comment la France manœuvre pour éviter une sortie de la RDC. Kinshasa menace de reconsidérer sa place au sein de l’Organisation internationale de la francophonie (OIF) si la Rwandaise Louise Mushikiwabo obtient un troisième mandat. Paris s’active en coulisses pour éviter qu’une crise ouverte fragilise l’organisation.

Moïse Katumbi veut aller à Goma, la défaite de Donald Trump et ses effets en Afrique, le blocage budgétaire au Sénégal… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la tournée diplomatique de Moïse Katumbi et de la coalition C64 en RDC, mesure les conséquences pour l’Afrique de la défaite de Donald Trump aux élections de mi-mandat, s’intéresse au rejet de la loi de finances rectificative par l’Assemblée nationale sénégalaise, évoque le parcours de Mary Vilakazi, première femme à la tête de FirstRand, et décrypte l’après-Minurso au Sahara.

Diasporas africaines : comment les États cherchent à capter les milliards qui irriguent le continent. Avec 124,2 milliards de dollars reçus en 2025, les transferts de la diaspora africaine dépassent largement l’aide au développement. Mais derrière cette manne inégalement répartie, le coût des envois demeure le plus élevé au monde. Décryptage en infographies.

Maroc : comment les réseaux sociaux transforment les migrations irrégulières vers l’Europe. Et si le passage des frontières se jouait désormais aussi sur les écrans ? Face aux nouvelles formes de mobilisation migratoire, Rabat adapte sa stratégie avec l’appui de Bruxelles. Pendant ce temps, la justice espagnole continue de chercher à savoir qui savait quoi lors de la crise de Ceuta, fin juillet.
En Guinée, l’opposant Aliou Bah libéré après 23 mois de détention. Condamné en janvier 2025 à deux ans de prison, l’opposant guinéen Aliou Bah a finalement été libéré ce 6 novembre.

En Afrique du Sud, le pari fou de « grand-mère » Helen Zille, candidate hors norme à la mairie de Johannesburg. L’ancienne édile du Cap et ex-présidente de l’Alliance démocratique pourrait devenir la première maire blanche de la capitale économique sud-africaine depuis la fin de l’apartheid, lors des élections municipales du mercredi 4 novembre.

« Ce n’est pas la fin du monde » : l’Afrique du Sud minimise la portée de son exclusion d’un accord commercial avec les Etats-Unis. Washington a fait savoir, lundi 2 novembre, que Pretoria ne bénéficiera plus de l’accord AGOA, qui exempte de taxes de nombreux produits africains importés aux Etats-Unis, à compter du 1ᵉʳ janvier 2027. Une décision attendue par l’exécutif, mais qui inquiète certains secteurs exposés.

En Afrique du Sud, la déconfiture annoncée de l’ANC, en perte de vitesse dans les grandes villes du pays. Chômage, criminalité, déliquescence des infrastructures, corruption… Le pays, dirigé depuis 1994 par le Congrès national africain, est rongé par de multiples crises. Le parti est annoncé au coude-à-coude avec l’Alliance démocratique lors du scrutin municipal de mercredi 4 novembre.

Au Sénégal, le débat sur les finances publiques vire au blocage institutionnel. Le premier ministre sénégalais, Ahmadou Al Aminou Mohamed Lô, essuie un nouveau revers. Sa loi de finances rectificative pour 2026, calibrée pour répondre aux attentes du FMI, a été rejetée par l’Assemblée nationale, mardi 3 novembre, pour la troisième fois.

Au Sénégal, la douloureuse mémoire des « années d’ajustement structurel » ressurgit après l’accord conclu avec le FMI. Le 1er septembre, Dakar et l’institution de Bretton Woods ont trouvé un agrément en vue d’un programme d’aide de près de 1,9 milliard d’euros. Un accord qui rappelle l’époque des réformes économiques strictes conduites dans les années 1980 et 1990.

Le Rwanda, ancien partenaire modèle des Etats-Unis, désormais dans le collimateur de l’administration Trump. Washington a annoncé, lundi 2 novembre, l’exclusion de Kigali de l’accord commercial préférentiel AGOA, à compter du 1ᵉʳ janvier 2027. Une décision brusque liée à l’implication du régime rwandais dans la guerre en cours dans l’est de la République démocratique du Congo.

En RDC, l’OMS alerte sur la « pire épidémie de choléra depuis des décennies », avec 1 800 morts, sur fond de crise liée à Ebola. Selon l’OMS, 2025 avait enregistré le nombre de cas signalés le plus élevé depuis plus de vingt-cinq ans, mais « l’année en cours s’annonce encore plus grave ».

Le Maroc mise sur le dessalement pour soutenir son agriculture d’exportation : « Il vaut mieux avoir de l’eau chère que pas du tout ». Dans la région du Souss-Massa, près d’Agadir, des milliers d’hectares de cultures destinées à l’exportation sont irrigués depuis 2022 grâce au dessalement de l’eau de mer. Un modèle que le royaume veut dupliquer en dépit de ses impacts écologiques et budgétaires.

En Tunisie, dans les camps de migrants d’El-Amra, une économie de la survie abandonnée à la violence. Au nord de Sfax, les migrants subsahariens sont régulièrement agressés par des bandes qui tentent de capter la manne financière dont ils disposent pour effectuer les traversées vers l’Italie. Fin octobre, deux Gambiens en ont été victimes.

Sahara occidental : « L’échec de la diplomatie risque de renforcer la frange du Front Polisario favorable à l’escalade militaire avec le Maroc ». L’analyste Riccardo Fabiani explique, dans un entretien au « Monde », que le retrait de la mission onusienne de maintien de la paix dans le territoire sahraoui, le 1ᵉʳ novembre, pourrait se traduire sur le terrain par une dégradation de la situation sécuritaire.

Nigeria : la justice annule la candidature à l’élection présidentielle de l’opposant Atiku Abubakar. Le candidat du Congrès démocratique africain était arrivé deuxième à l’élection présidentielle de 2023 avec 29 % des voix.

En Somalie, la Cour suprême juge « illégal » le maintien au pouvoir du président Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. Mercredi, le chef de l’Etat avait annoncé sur Facebook avoir « démis de ses fonctions » le président de la Cour suprême, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, « en réponse aux préoccupations exprimées par les juges ».

Municipales en Afrique du Sud : l’ANC obtient environ 30 % des voix, son pire score, après 80 % du dépouillement. Le score du Congrès national africain est particulièrement scruté en vue du congrès du parti devant désigner à sa tête dans un an le successeur de Cyril Ramaphosa, l’actuel chef d’Etat.

Au Kenya, le gourou qui encourageait ses disciples à mourir de faim pour « rencontrer Jésus » condamné à deux cents ans de prison. Les médias ont rapidement appelé cette affaire le « massacre de la forêt de Shakahola », une des pires tragédies liées à des dérives sectaires qui a traumatisé le pays d’Afrique de l’Est.

Au Nigeria, Atiku Abubakar maintient sa candidature à la présidentielle malgré l’annulation par la justice. Jeudi, un tribunal d’Abuja a annulé la candidature de celui qui brigue pour la septième fois la magistrature suprême en invalidant toutes les décisions prises par le président de sa formation politique, le Congrès démocratique africain (ADC), jugé illégitime.
Kenya : deux cents ans de prison pour le gourou Paul Mackenzie. Le pasteur autoproclamé a été reconnu responsable du meurtre de 190 enfants et d’un adulte.

A Makalé, capitale d’un Tigré retombé aux mains de l’armée éthiopienne, l’écho persistant de la guerre. La ville a été reprise par l’armée fédérale le 3 octobre. Chassés de leur fief historique, les rebelles tigréens se sont retranchés dans les zones montagneuses de la région. Covering Palestine: Historic news clippings reveal US media complicity in Israel's crimes Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Wed, 10/28/2026 - 13:45 An archive of American newspaper excerpts documents how Israel’s occupation was reported before 7 October 2023 A clipping from the San Francisco Examiner with the headline “Arab activist killed by Santa Ana bomb” from 12 October 1985 Off For years, mainstream media has been criticised for its failure to report accurately on Israel ’s genocide in Gaza, allowing Israel to commit crimes with impunity. In July the UN special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories, Fransesca Albanese, released a report about the media complicity in genocide. Her report details how the systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists, Israeli media’s incitement, and the legitimisation from international coverage have facilitated genocide and obstructed accountability. Outlets relied heavily on Israeli sources, using the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 to justify Israel’s subsequent onslaught and present the conflict as though it began exclusively with the attack. It was frustration with this narrative that prompted Maria Robles, an independent researcher and artist, to begin research into archival American newspaper stories. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); She wanted to “share the reality” of what was happening in Palestine through “public history and public memory - not based on opinion, but aggregating existing materials, existing research, existing journalism and making it as accessible as possible to the public”. Over three years, Robles collated more than 3,000 clippings from almost 700 papers dating from 1724 to 2023, using online archives and physical records, and in doing so, establishing Covering Palestine . Robles had previously worked on a research campaign to raise awareness about the history of slavery in New York using publicly available archive material. “Covering Palestine similarly is about education or access to it, being a tool. So is data,” she told Middle East Eye. “I think both of them move us toward liberation, one step at a time.” The website allows users to filter material by year, newspaper and subject, tracing patterns , names and key events. She hopes the archive will help the public understand Palestine’s history prior to 2023 and allow researchers and organisations to “look and understand, criticise and question how the information was shared, and talked about and reported on”. From 'colonisation' to 'settlement' “The media bias has always been there,” Robles explained, but the language used has changed with the times: for example, it was striking that Israel was discussed explicitly as a colonial project when the term was less of a dirty word. “Plan of colonising Palestine with Jews,” one New York Times headline announced on 6 January 1902. “Jews set up six colonies,” another said on 24 May 1939. In pictures: Life in Palestine from 1890 to 1937 Read More » In 1926, the Buffalo Jewish Review reported that “Jewish Colonisation will Extend Beyond Palestine Frontier”. Covering Palestine traces how the word “colonisation” became controversial and was replaced with “settlement”; a shift beginning in the 1920s, with the term having mostly disappeared by 1948. Today, critics accuse papers such as the New York Times (NYT) of routinely whitewashing Israeli imperialism, comparing headlines describing Israel’s illegal occupation of southern Lebanon as “ cementing its foothold ” or “ plans to control ” with much less euphemistic ones about the Russian invasion of Ukraine. In an NYT opinion piece, columnist Bret Stephens dismissed the description of Israel as a settler-colonial state as “invidious, hypocritical and historically illiterate” and called Zionism “the oldest continuous anticolonial movement in history”, contradicting how the paper he wrote in once presented it. The passive voice A 2024 study from The Intercept found a clear pro-Israel bias in mainstream media coverage, particularly the NYT, with outlets consistently applying a double standard when using emotive words such as “massacre” and “slaughter” to describe civilian deaths. During the first 100 days of the conflict following 7 October, the NYT used the word “massacre” 124 times to describe violence against Israelis and never against Palestinians; during the first year, CNN used it 225 times for Israelis and 16 times for Palestinians - despite a far higher Palestinian death toll. Palestinian deaths, meanwhile, are frequently reported on using the passive voice: a headline from the Washington Post read “Israel’s war in Gaza claims thousands of young lives”. Another stated “more than 1,000 people have been killed in Gaza during ceasefire, Palestinian authorities say”. This pattern is not new. On 29 October 1956, Israeli border police shot dead 48 unarmed Palestinian civilians, including 23 children, in Kafr Qasim , who were returning home from their fields for violating a curfew imposed by the Israeli army on the town earlier that day that they had not been informed of. Covering Palestine’s archive revealed all too familiar patterns of passive and euphemistic language The story was suppressed by Israeli military censorship for 44 days. Nothing on Kafr Qasim appears in the archive until 12 December 1956, the day David Ben-Gurion, the prime minister, broke his own ban and told the Knesset. Of the papers in the archive that carried the disclosure, not one put “massacre” in a headline, and it was not until 13 October 1958 , after a military court had convicted eight border police, that the word appeared in a headline to describe the event. When reports eventually emerged, Covering Palestine’s archive revealed all too familiar patterns of passive and euphemistic language. “Israel Discloses Killing of Arabs In Curfew Tift” was how Oregon’s News Review reported on the incident on 12 December 1956. Meanwhile, the New York Newsday labelled it “Bare Slaying by Error of 48 Israeli Arabs”: indicating the event was accidental before any investigation had been opened. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); One New York Times headline said “48 Arabs Killed; Israel Penitent”. Alongside a scan of the clipping, Robles transcribed the headline, adding citations for researchers and linking to further context. She noted the NYT headline was the only one that led with the death toll, but used the passive “killed”, without naming the perpetrator, before turning to “the condition of Israel’s conscience”. Censorship In April 2024, a leaked NYT memo instructed journalists to avoid terms including “genocide”, “ethnic cleansing” and “occupied territory” in their reporting on the conflict. Robles noted that historical reports were often explicit about Israeli censorship: a 1980 NYT article declared “Israeli Censorship Strikes a Discordant, Insistent Note”, beginning “this dispatch has been subjected to Israeli censorship”. By contrast, she said, “now…the reporting has to rationalise, maybe not successfully…why they are reporting it the way they are”, repeating Israeli talking points without acknowledging them, such as “Israel’s right to defend itself” or claims Hamas uses civilians as “ human shields ”. The censorship of the Palestinian press was also reported on by the New York Times, detailing how “Israel Tightens Control Over Arab Newspapers” when Israeli authorities intercepted trucks and confiscated papers being transported for distribution in the West Bank in 1982. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Today, Palestinians document the genocide committed against them directly through social media, reaching international audiences without their language being filtered through American media or Israeli censorship. However, Israel’s systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists has made Gaza the deadliest place to be a journalist. The early reports of Palestinian newspapers being shut down are reflected in Israel’s attacks on journalists today, Robles explained, “not allowing [Palestinians] the opportunity to do their own reporting or speak about what is happening”. Israel frequently labels Palestinian journalists “terrorists” to justify these attacks - lies that their western colleagues uncritically echo without adequate scrutiny. Dehumanisation Similarly, strikes on Gaza are often reported as “targeting Hamas”, regardless of civilian casualties, while death tolls are attributed to Gaza’s “Hamas-run health ministry”, casting doubt on their reliability. Yet long before Hamas existed, American papers used dehumanising language to rationalise Israel’s atrocities, diminishing their readers’ empathy for Palestinian victims. In July 1972, Palestinian novelist Ghassan Kanafani was killed alongside his teenage niece by a bomb planted in his car in Beirut. Reporting on his death, US news outlets presented him as an “Arab Militant leader”, “Revolutionary”, or “ Palestinian Guerrilla ”, with only one headline in 11 calling him an artist, according to Robles. Ghassan Kanafani: The life of a Palestinian writer Read More » A central motivation behind Covering Palestine was to humanise Palestinians by documenting their experiences across generations, including rare occasions when they were named or their lives and culture covered without the association with death and suffering. “That humanising of people…reminding [the public] that these are really people that these experiences are really happening to” is important to counteract the dehumanisation they face, Robles said. She also wanted to challenge Zionist myths that Palestine was a “land without people” or not a real country. The historical record reveals a people and community that existed for many years prior to Israel’s establishment: one clipping from 1891 described “the Fellaheen [peasants] of Palestine” as “an ancient and historic people”; similarly in 1910 they were referred to as “the aboriginal inhabitants of the Holy Land”. As genocide seeks to eradicate a people and their past, Robles wants to use Covering Palestine to preserve and expose the history of a place whose story began long before 7 October. Rains flood Gaza displacement camps as Israeli authorities block entry of shelter materials into territory Thousands of tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded by heavy rains overnight, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation. Scarce aid entering the territory has left tens of thousands of Palestinians in the war-torn enclave exposed to the elements for a fourth winter in a row- with no fuel and nothing but makeshift tents and shelters for protection. Red Cross spokesperon Amani Al Naouq told Al Jazeera that she has seen footage of “entire families, entire camps” inundated with water and scrambling to drain their tents and protect their belongings and lives. In October, Director General for the International Organization for Migration Amy Pope warned that nearly all of Gaza's population require shelter assistance, with the combined supply pipeline of humanitarian shelter partners covering barely 17 per cent of identified winter needs. "Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," Pope said. "Shelter materials must enter quickly, predictably and at the scale required." Israel has continued to tightly restrict the entry of aid into the territory, with shelter items- including tent poles, construction materials and mobile homes- almost completely barred as the Israeli authorities consider them "dual use" items. IOM said that around 8,600 IOM emergency shelter kits are waiting outside Gaza, but continue to be turned away from crossing points by the Israeli authorities. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs346 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs378. The prices are applicable from Nov 7 (Saturday) to Nov 10 (Tuesday) due to a public holiday on Nov 9, according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

When home is hell. ON an ordinary March afternoon this year, the children of a household in Lahore’s Choong district gathered for their uncle’s small promise of treats. Among them was four-year-old Azan, who was led out for a stroll by his uncle. It all ended eight hours later in the isolated outskirts of Quaid-i-Azam Industrial Estate — with Azan dead. The minor’s body, when recovered, showed a two-inch exposed spinal cord attaching the head and mutilated remains. Azan had reportedly been tortured and eventually killed with an eight-inch-long knife by his own father, allegedly in a calculated bid to implicate a third party. Azan is just one of several children who are killed every month by people known to them. Moving back, in October, a 13-year-old in Mianwali was shot dead by her cousin for not wearing a hijab. In September, a three-year-old in Islamabad was kidnapped, raped, and murdered by her brother-in-law. In August, an 18-month-old in Karachi died after being raped by her 17-year-old cousin, while in July, a six-year-old boy was beaten up, raped, and strangled with a wire by his neighbour, and a four-year-old girl in Gujranwala was set on fire by her mother on suspicion of being ‘possessed’. In May, a father in Vehari repeatedly raped his three daughters aged 14, 11, and nine for six consecutive months; while three children aged six, four, and three were killed and found hanging from the fans in their home in Multan. A month earlier, in April, a mother in Lahore brutally slit the throats of her three children, luring them through a sadistic ‘game’ of hide-and-seek. Occurring within the safe confines of the home, these tragedies shocked and enraged us more than others, but our protest ended in quiet resignation, as it did in 2022 when an eight-year-old was tortured and poisoned by her grandparents for failing at household chores, and in 2015 when a 12-year-old was beaten to death by her father for not making properly round rotis. Homes repeatedly turn into hell for children as our criminal justice system is unequipped to intercept and prevent attacks within the home. Statutes such as the ICT and Sindh Child Protection Acts create institutional bodies that address minors’ welfare, but they lack the authority to adopt anticipatory, prompt, and intrusive measures to ensure child safety. Our laws are reactive rather than anticipatory. Even the landmark Zainab Alert, Response, and Recovery Act, 2020, creates a protection mechanism for missing children that is enforceable only after the abduction is reported. As a result, attacks on children in public are not easily prevented. Our criminal justice system is unequipped to intercept and prevent attacks within the home. Recently, a five-year-old in Haripur was raped and left to die after being lured out of her home to see her father; an eight-year-old in Lahore was sexually harassed in a grocery store by the owner, and an eight-year-old in Sargodha was raped and murdered in a grocery store. Even when these victims were seen being accompanied or coaxed by a group of men or being eyed by strangers, the palpable threat of attack was ignored by those present at the scene. It was also in the presence of bystanders in Multan that 15-year-old Wasim was tortured and then run over by his employer recently. Whether it was their indifference or ignorance, they abandoned the weakest, most vulnerable members of society — our children. Being voiceless, defenceless and weak, children are considered dispensable. It is, therefore, easy to ignore injustices against them. We tolerate inadequate child protection laws and mechanisms, ignore the proliferation of pornographic content, disregard paedophilic customs such as trading minor boys, and permit appalling lectures advocating marriage with girls as young as four. Our complicity and apathy have normalised child abuse and allowed it to persist, putting Pakistan third on the global map for child abuse. Around 2,000 cases of child abuse were reported in just the first six months of the current year. Sahil reported over 3,600 in 2025. In 2024, 21 children were being abused daily. Reducing such horrifying figures demands enforceable protection under the law. Justice Jawad Hasan in 2023 (Zafar Khizer vs the Federation of Pakistan)initiated a shift in discourse from viewing children as ordinary citizens to viewing them as vulnerable citizens categorised as ‘child citizens’ and entitled to a higher degree of protection and concern under the law. Justice Usman G. Rashid last month said that the child citizen is entitled to fundamental rights in their independent capacity that cannot be displaced by any parental authority. While the concept of the child citizen as an independent rights holder is evolving through jurisprudence, it is insufficient without effective implementation and accountability. Mandatory reporting regimes should be introduced for designated professionals such as healthcare providers, instructors, and adults in child-related roles or positions of trust, as under Australian law and England’s Crime and Policing Act, 2026. Additional measures for prevention through reporting suspected child abuse and conducting child-sensitive investigations and follow-ups in such cases must be made compulsory in line with the spirit of Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. These obligations must be rooted not merely in law, but in a shared sense of humanity and a collective duty to protect the vulnerable because, as lawyer and human rights activist Asma Jahangir said, a society that fails to protect its children has, in fact, failed humanity’s most basic test. The writer is a lawyer. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

SC calls for scrutiny of illegal power connections. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Friday underlined the need for a microscopic examination of the role of individuals involved in the theft, unauthorised sale and private siphoning of electricity, rather than supplying it through authorised channels. The observation came from a two-judge SC bench, comprising Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar and Justice Irfan Saadat Khan, which was hearing a bail-cancellation petition in a case where a person suffered an electric shock after a power wire snapped. In a six-page order, Justice Mazhar emphasised the need for a thorough examination of current practices by Wapda and the concerned utility companies, observing that it was inconceivable that electricity could be supplied without the knowledge of Wapda, or the concerned utility company and its officials. Petitioner Ali Asghar Khokhar, a resident of Khuhawar Street, Larkana, had filed a criminal petition before the SC seeking cancellation of bail granted to respondent Anwar Ali Kori by the Sindh High Court’s Larkana circuit bench on Oct 20, 2025. Wonders how ‘unauthorised’ supply rackets run under Wapda officials’ noses The case stemmed from an incident in March 2024, when Noor Hussain, the petitioner’s brother, suffered an electric shock after a PVC wire broke and came into contact with a high-tension line. Subsequently, an FIR was registered at Rehmatpur police station in Larkana against Anwar Ali Kori and other Wapda officials. The allegation was that the co-accused, including Wapda officials and the respondent, were supplying electricity to people in their shops by laying a special line from the disposal phase line and running an electric wire over the complainant’s shops. The complainant, who appeared in person before the SC, argued that the high court had granted bail without examining the facts and the incriminating material collected by the investigating officer (IO). However, the SC noted that the high court had granted bail to the respondent predominantly on the grounds of a nine-month delay in lodging the FIR, besides the fact that the role attributed to the respondent was one of negligence. Furthermore, the high court’s order also reflected the IO’s statement that the respondent had no contact with Wapda officials. Therefore, after considering the relevant factors, the high court had reached the tentative assessment that the allegations levelled in the FIR required further inquiry and accordingly confirmed the bail order, the SC observed. It added that the matter at hand also required further inquiry and that, unless a full-dress trial was conducted, the role and guilt of the accused persons implicated in the case could not be established. The SC recalled that, when the complainant was asked how he was powering his shop, he said the respondent was working as a contractor in collusion with Wapda officials and supplying electricity to his shop against monetary consideration. He added that he had never been issued a bill by Wapda or any other utility company. However, after arguing at some length, the complainant himself stated that since the trial was pending, he did not wish to press for cancellation of the respondent’s bail. The SC observed that the high court’s order granting bail did not require any interference and directed the court office to transmit a copy of the order to the Wapda chairman for information. Party office-bearers, workers, religious scholars, political and social figures participated in the demonstrations, expressing their solidarity with the Maulana. Addressing the gatherings, speakers praised the Maulana’s role in safeguarding the Constitution, democracy, parliamentary supremacy, religious values and public rights. They said the alleged aerial surveillance of his private residence through a drone and the subsequent circulation of the footage on social media were unacceptable in any civilised society. Such actions, they argued, could intensify political tensions and create unrest and resentment in society. They demanded an immediate, transparent and impartial investigation into the alleged drone filming of Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s residence. They called for those responsible, including the individuals allegedly involved behind the scenes, to be identified and dealt with in accordance with the law. They also condemned the use of social media for character assassination, false allegations and organized negative campaigns instead of promoting political debate and public awareness. They stressed that those involved in such activities must be brought to justice. Terming them acts of government panic and political vendetta, the gathering insisted that the Maulana and his party were being subjected to vindictive action for raising their voice against the “Form 47 government”, for the unity of the provinces, the NFC Award and the possible 18th Constitutional Amend­ment, and against what they termed conspiracies to seize the provinces’ mineral resources. They stressed, however, that the party would not be intimidated and would continue its constitutional, legal and democratic struggle. The meeting announced that, on the directive of the party chief and in line with a policy of non-violence, protests would be held on highways and major roads. Transparency in investments Meanwhile, addressing a gathering of the Jamiat Talaba Islam in Islamabad, the Maulana called for transparency in agreements with foreign investors, particularly those involving Pakistan’s mineral resources, stressing that the country’s natural wealth should not be exploited through secret arrangements at the expense of its people. He said his party was not oppo­sed to investment from China, the US or multinational companies, but all agreements must be made public, with clearly defined shares of profits for Pakistan, foreign investors and local communities. “We are not against anyone’s inv­estment, but there must be transparency in the process and agreements. The nation should be informed about the conditions under which contracts are signed,” he said. The Maulana also alleged that the government was using security measures in tribal districts to facilitate illegal trade routes. Referring to recurring curfews in parts of the tribal belt, he questioned why restrictions were im­­posed for two days a week while the remaining five days were apparently considered free of terrorism. Bavaria’s speaker tipped to become Germany’s first woman president. GERMAN Chancellor Friedrich Merz (left) shakes hands with Ilse Aigner, the speaker of Bavaria’s state parliament, upon arrival at the Christian Social Union party’s congress in Munich.—AFP BERLIN: Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner is expected to become Germany’s next president in 2027, the first woman to serve as its head of state, conservative ruling party sources said on Friday. Aigner, 61, now the speaker of the southern state’s regional assembly, would replace outgoing President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, a Social Democrat, in the largely ceremonial post. Steinmeier, who took office in 2017, will reach the limit of two five-year terms in March next year. Aigner belongs to the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of the centre-right CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is supporting the choice of Aigner, the party sources said. If her nomination is confirmed at a CDU/CSU meeting on Monday, she would be all but certain to be formally elected on Jan 30 by both houses of parliament and civil society representatives. Aigner’s political appeal owes much to a trademark Bavarian warmth, and her appearances in a traditional dirndl dress at beer festivals have made her a familiar figure across the state. Supporters see her consensual approach as an asset in an increasingly polarised country, where the far-right, anti-immigration and pro-Russian AfD party has reached record levels of popularity. LHC rejects plea for directions to legislation on marital rape. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) has dismissed a public interest petition seeking directions to the federal and provincial governments to legislate on marital rape, holding that a constitutional court cannot compel the legislature to enact a particular law or create a new offence. Justice Abher Gul Khan clarified that the ruling neither endorses violence or abuse within marriage, nor prevents the Parliament or any provincial assembly from taking up the matter. Areej Sohail Bhutta, a lawyer, filed the petition, stating that she had encountered women clients who complained of non-consensual sexual conduct within their marriages. She argued that the law lacked a distinct statutory framework for sexual violence within marriage. She sought directions for legislative measures, including amendments to sections 375 and 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code. A court can’t force the legislature to enact a law or create an offence, observes the judge Justice Khan observed that the Constitution divides powers among the legislature, the executive and the judiciary, and that judicial review does not authorise courts to assume legislative functions. She said Article 199 empowers the high court to issue directions for the enforcement of fundamental rights. However, she maintained, there is a distinction between directing an authority to perform an existing constitutional or statutory obligation and compelling the legislature to enact a particular law or create a new offence. The judge noted that articles 9, 14 and 25 protect the security, dignity and equality of a person, while articles 25(3) and 34 allow special protections for women and promote their participation in national life. She said Article 35, which requires the state to protect marriage and the family, does not provide a licence for violence against a spouse. Justice Khan observed that foreign laws can provide comparative guidance, but cannot override Pakistan’s Constitution or replace the judgment of its legislature. She said any proposed legal framework also has to be examined in the light of the Constitution, existing laws and the injunctions of Islam. The judge noted that under Article 142(b), the Parliament and provincial assemblies are competent to legislate on criminal law, procedure and evidence. “The question whether an additional offence, a separate statutory provision or a further protective mechanism is required, is essentially a matter of legislative policy,” the judge observed. Citing Supreme Court judgments, including Tika Iqbal Muhammad Khan versus Pervez Musharraf (PLJ 2008 SC 500), the judge observed, “A court cannot issue a mandamus compelling the legislature to enact a particular law.” The judge noted that the petitioner had neither challenged a specific statutory provision as unconstitutional nor identified an authority’s failure to perform an existing legal duty. She said the relief sought would require the court to direct legislation according to a model proposed by the petitioner, amounting to interference in the legislative process. The judge stressed that the decision does not diminish a woman’s dignity or bodily integrity because of marriage, or endorse coercion and abuse within marriage. The judge dismissed the petition to the extent of the relief sought. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

Nepra raises industrial tariff to Rs25.30 per unit, despite dissent. • Two members oppose revision, saying actual marginal cost stands at Rs31.83/unit • Power regulator warns of package suspension and legal action over missed deadlines • Consumers to pay an additional Rs2.37/unit in Nov bills to recover Rs25bn under fuel cost adjustment ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) on Friday announced a controversial revision of a special electricity tariff introduced as an incentive to revive industrial activity, while approving an additional burden of Rs2.37 per unit on electricity consumers for November. The decision, opposed by the industrial sector, is likely to have a negative impact on all electricity consumers, including those served by K-Electric and other distribution companies (Discos). All four members of the regulator unanimously held the Power Division and its subordinate entities responsible for failing to fulfil their legal obligations within the prescribed timelines, pushing Nepra into an unprecedented deadlock and potentially increasing costs for electricity consumers across the country. At the centre of the controversy was an incremental support package (ISP) of Rs22.98 per unit introduced for industrial consumers in December last year. Industrialists have been protesting against the package since May, seeking its suspension on the grounds that it had failed to benefit them and was instead increasing their electricity bills. The package was due for a review after the completion of its first six months in June, based on the lessons learnt during its implementation. Following a belated request from the Power Division, despite repeated reminders from the regulator, Nepra on Friday revised the ISP rate to Rs25.30 per unit. The decision was strongly opposed by its two most relevant members, those responsible for tariff and development matters. Interestingly, Nepra Chairman Waseem Mukhtar fully endorsed the written arguments and positions taken by the dissenting members but subsequently exercised his special casting vote to approve the revised rate of Rs25.30 per unit instead of retaining the existing rate of Rs22.98. The authority was divided 2-2 on the matter. Member Tariff Amina Ahmed and Member Development Maqsood Anwar, in a joint dissenting note, maintained that even the proposed revised rate of Rs25.30 per unit was a “random number” unsupported by evidence. They said Nepra’s own institutional calculations put the marginal cost at Rs31.83 per unit rather than Rs25.30. “The revised incremental rate of Rs25.30 per unit proposed by the Ministry of Energy (MoE), and allowed by the honourable Chairman and Member (Law), is based on the generation mix apparently assumed at the design stage of the package, with updated fuel prices,” the two members observed. They called for the immediate suspension of the ISP until authentic data became available. The dissenting members argued that compliance with the federal cabinet’s decision and Nepra’s own directives required a reassessment of the existing rate of Rs22.98 per unit to determine whether it should be retained, revised or suspended. However, this exercise had not been carried out, resulting in the continuation of the package at a rate below the actual cost of supplying incremental electricity. “The resulting misalignment has had implications for consumers in two ways. First, to the extent incremental consumption increased the system’s average fuel cost, the resulting impact was recovered from all consumers through the FCA mechanism. Second, because incremental units are excluded from quarterly tariff adjustments, the exclusion of such units increases the quarterly adjustment borne by consumers not availing the package,” they said. The two members, therefore, recommended the temporary suspension of the tariff package rather than choosing the proposed rate of Rs25.30 or above per unit. They questioned how a package based on the principle of cost-reflectivity could continue without a validated cost-reflective rate. They argued that since the alternative rate had no credible link with the actual marginal cost, continuation of the package was no longer justified. They said other consumers should not be made to bear the cost of a review that the MoE was required to submit five months ago but had yet to provide. In his casting vote, Nepra Chairman Waseem Mukhtar observed that the dissenting members’ conclusions “need serious consideration”. However, he said suspending the package at this stage would not be appropriate and that the Ministry of Energy should be given another opportunity to provide the information repeatedly sought by the regulator, including in its latest determination. All four members agreed that the Power Division was required to submit revised calculations six months ago but had failed to do so despite repeated reminders from Nepra. They also regretted that the ministry had not responded adequately to the questions and queries raised by the regulator. “The marginal price, in proper form, was not provided to the regulator by either the Independent System and Market Operator (ISMO) or the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC), which were duty-bound to do so. Since the ISP is a flagship project of the ministry, it should give due consideration to the observations of Nepra and the lack of inter-agency coordination among the entities working under the ministry,” the members observed. The determination also sets deadlines for the relevant entities to provide the required information. The four members warned that failure to meet these deadlines could lead to an adverse outcome in the review of the programme, including its suspension or termination. “Furthermore, any entity that fails to provide the required information within the stipulated timeline shall lead to initiation of legal proceedings under the applicable legal framework,” they stated. Explaining his decision, Nepra chairman said: “I hereby exercise, in due and faithful discharge of the functions of the Authority, my second and casting vote envisaged and entrusted to me under the Nepra Act in favour of the First Opinion, thereby breaking the deadlock in relation to the aforesaid issues. Accordingly, the First Opinion constitutes the Order of the Authority.” Meanwhile, Nepra allowed power distribution companies to charge an additional Rs2.37 per unit from all consumers in their November bills under the monthly fuel cost adjustment (FCA) mechanism to recover an additional Rs25 billion.
