Punjab Revenue Authority wants electronic invoice system at all hotels, restaurants. LAHORE: Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) has sought all hotels and restaurants to be equipped with the electronic invoice monitoring system (EIMS) for timely payment of taxes. It was sought by the authorities in a meeting with the Hotels and Restaurant Association held here on Friday. During the meeting, matters concerning installation of EIMS in the hotel industry and tax compliance came under discussion. The meeting focused on measures to bring the entire hotel industry into the tax net and further broaden the tax base. The participants reviewed the EIMS installation process, technical requirements and challenges faced by hotels in implementing the system. The association office-bearers assured the PRA of its full cooperation in initiatives aimed at improving the tax system and promoting digitalisation. On this occasion, PRA Chairperson Moazzam Iqbal Sipra emphasised that issuing proper computerised receipts to customers against services provided was a legal requirement. He stated that with the cooperation of the business community, the tax system could be made simpler, more transparent and efficient. He further noted that expanding the tax net would encourage business activities and promote a culture of tax compliance. The chairperson also warned that business operators involved in fraudulent practices in the issuance of electronic receipts would be closely monitored and subjected to heavy penalties. Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

Pakistan warns UN against weakening peacekeeping amid budget cuts. UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has urged the United Nations not to allow financial constraints and cost-cutting measures to weaken its peacekeeping operations, warning that reductions in resources could undermine the organisation’s ability to maintain international peace and security. The warning comes as UN peacekeeping faces mounting financial and political pressures. The General Assembly has approved a $5.1 billion budget for peacekeeping operations for 2026-27, about 10 per cent lower than the previous year’s allocation. A funding crisis last year had already forced the organisation to reduce mission expenditure and repatriate a quarter of its uniformed personnel from peacekeeping operations. Against this backdrop, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, called for reforms that improve the effectiveness of peacekeeping without sacrificing the capabilities needed to carry out its mandates. “What is needed is the political will in the Security Council to use this important instrument when circumstances require,” he told the Fourth Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on Friday. Pakistan is one of the largest and longest-serving contributors to UN peacekeeping. More than 170,000 Pakistani military and police personnel have served in UN missions over the past six decades, with 183 losing their lives . Pakistan also hosts the United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP). Ambassador Shah’s intervention comes at a time when peacekeeping operations are confronting not only financial difficulties but also increasingly complicated political and security environments. Growing reliance on regional arrangements and ad hoc operations, he argued, demonstrated that the need for a credible UN presence on the ground remained undiminished. Welcoming the secretary-general’s review of peacekeeping operations, Pakistan outlined six priorities for reform: giving primacy to political solutions; ensuring focused and adequately resourced mandates; preserving the institutional strengths of peacekeeping; preparing for future military and police requirements; improving the safety and security of peacekeepers; and maintaining peacekeeping as a collective UN responsibility. The central concern was the widening gap between the responsibilities assigned to peacekeeping missions and the resources made available to them. Pakistan cautioned against allowing financial ceilings to determine operational requirements. Political objectives, Ambassador Shah argued, should first establish what a mission is expected to accomplish. Its mandate should then determine the personnel, equipment and financial resources required. Peacekeeping missions can help stabilise conflict situations, protect civilians, sustain ceasefires and preserve space for negotiations. But these functions depend on political processes and adequate operational capabilities working together. Pakistan also urged member states to preserve the distinctive advantages of UN peacekeeping, including its universal legitimacy, predictable financing, established command and logistics systems, and ability to draw personnel and specialised capabilities from across the UN membership. “Efficiency and cost reduction must therefore strengthen peacekeeping, not hollow out the capabilities that give UN peacekeeping its unique value,” the ambassador said. The protection of peacekeepers and accountability for crimes committed against them formed another major part of Pakistan’s intervention. Pakistan, alongside Denmark, played a leading role in advancing UN Security Council Resolution 2823 , which was unanimously adopted with a record 153 co-sponsors. The resolution seeks to strengthen accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers, an issue Pakistan has repeatedly raised at the UN. Welcoming the secretary-general’s first report on accountability for crimes against peacekeepers, Ambassador Shah also noted the appointment of Assistant Secretary-General Elizabeth Spehar as Senior Focal Point on the matter. He called for the resolution’s effective implementation through stronger investigations and prosecutions, better tracking of cases and greater support for national capacities to ensure that those responsible for attacks on peacekeepers were brought to justice. Pakistan also stressed the importance of the Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations, known as C-34, describing it as the universal intergovernmental forum for collectively shaping peacekeeping policy. The consensus achieved within the committee, together with the broad support for Resolution 2823, demonstrated that member states continued to regard peacekeeping as an important instrument of international cooperation. Pakistan’s position was that reform should make peacekeeping more effective and adaptable to changing circumstances, rather than weaken the institution at a time when international conflicts and political divisions make its role increasingly important. “Peacekeeping remains a vital, effective and cost-efficient means for ensuring peace and security. We will need this instrument again. We should ensure that it is ready when we do,” Ambassador Shah concluded.

Iran says forces ‘stronger’ than at beginning of war. Iran said Saturday its military has grown “stronger” since the outset of its war with the United States, which has offered a $20 million reward for information about Tehran’s nuclear programme. Mediators have been working to prevent any resumption of fighting after months of deadlock in the Middle East conflict, which began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Tehran has sought to limit traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption. Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Tehran retained control over the strategic waterway and that it would remain closed until its demands were met by the US. He also said Iran’s forces had grown stronger and more confident, state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday. “Today, the Islamic Republic’s armed forces… having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war,” he said. “They now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence.” “Under the order of the Supreme Leader, the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective, and without geographical limitations,” he added. Reward offered The US military said it was offering a $20 million reward “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear programme. The programme was established in 1984 under the State Department’s national security rewards programme to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests. In a statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran’s “lack of compliance with the (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges.” It did not specify what type of information would warrant a $20 million reward. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said US forces have effectively obliterated Iran’s nuclear programme . “If we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today,” Trump said Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida. “If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East.” Dialogue The president also said Iran — which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war — is eager to end the conflict. “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” he said. Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on Friday to discuss efforts to end the war. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said this week his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue. Early on Saturday, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, adding there was no official information about any damage. Iranian state television reported two explosions on the island. The Iranian army said early Saturday that its air defences had “struck and destroyed” a US drone that was flying over the island, according to state media. It did not say whether the island was attacked.

Making the most of America’s midterm tsunami. Imagine, for a moment, that the US midterm elections had not delivered Democratic wins at a generational scale, but merely a trickle of flipped seats—enough, perhaps, to change control of the House of Representatives but not enough for a Senate majority. Is there any doubt that President Donald Trump would embrace such results as a good-enough validation of his often lawless and brutal administration? Would it not now be doubling down, striving to cast the polls as an imprimatur for its excesses? Instead, American democracy skirted a disabling blow. Yet it would be a grave mistake to take a further step by concluding that voters’ overwhelming rejection of Trump and his Republican Party marks a full-throated public re-embrace of democracy. The election was a disaster averted, but it was only an opening to assess and fix the damage caused by two years of a rogue administration acting without congressional oversight. The Democrats’ landslide victory could set America’s now clearly imperfect democracy on the difficult path of repair and improvement. But this opportunity could slip away unless seized swiftly. Conventional wisdom about the midterm results is already resurrecting James Carville’s old adage: “It’s the economy, stupid.” There is, indeed, a kernel of truth to this. The Associated Press exit poll conducted on election day flagged economic discontent as voters’ top concern. Likewise, a Gallup poll from a week beforehand also found voters ranking inflation and health care as the most important issues. Against this backdrop, the bizarre optics of Trump’s midterm campaigning—Look at my reflecting pool! My beautiful ballroom! What about Jon Husted’s great butt!—underscore Trump’s surreal detachment from everyday voters’ woes. So potent is this story that most influential media outlets are offering inflation and affordability as catch-all explanations for the Democrats’ sweep through states Republicans had held for decades. And it is easy to see this simple story becoming a guiding light for anti-Trump figures, including among Republicans, for the next two years. This emerging consensus captures an important part of the story, but also overlooks an important finding. According to the AP exit poll, almost one-third of voters named the health of democracy as their top concern—just six points behind the economy—while the Gallup poll appears not to have asked respondents about the issue at all. Concerns over democracy and the rule of law also help explain the massive swings among Hispanic and Black voters. A UnidosUS survey of Hispanics found that immigration “overreach”—that is, flagrant disregard for the rule of law—was a leading concern. Anecdotal evidence suggests that Black turnout was driven by anger at the dismantling of the landmark 1965 Voting Rights Act—that is, by outrage at right-wing judges’ frontal assault on multiracial democracy. The affordability narrative risks overshadowing this strong public demand for democracy and even erasing it from the shared public memory of this election. That understanding of history creates a trap for Democrats, leaving the new House and Senate majorities a hostage to fortune, or worse. While control of the House and the Senate offers them a few policy tools with which to address inflation and affordability, those tools may not work quickly, and Trump retains broad control over trade policy and war-making. Indeed, because Trump can still make things worse, it is reasonable to think that there will be scant improvement in economic sentiment two years from now. No doubt, the Republican presidential nominee in 2028 will pin the blame on the Democrats. At a minimum, the picture will be muddy. Despite this risk, the affordability narrative is seductive to many Democrats, because it means they don’t need to think about the structural problems with American democracy. Consider here rampant electoral gerrymandering, the Senate’s malapportionment favoring rural populations, and the egregious inflation of judicial power. This time, the size of the Democratic wave overcame those barriers. But it would be reckless to count on that in the future, particularly as Trump retains powerful tools to erode democratic norms further. The Democrats, then, would be wise to lean into the democracy message by pressing for more structural change—not only because it is the principled thing to do, but also because it is in their political interest. This does not mean simply focusing on the Trump family’s venality. Highlighting corruption can be politically effective, as the midterm results showed. But unless the strong linkage between corruption and a weakening of democracy is made explicit—how the scramble for spoils overcomes representation of voters and their interests—scandalous revelations can also breed disabling cynicism and even voter apathy. The US midterm election results are an opportunity and an invitation. Voters’ demand for the rule of law and democracy has helped destroy Trump’s MAGA movement. That demand must not be forgotten or suppressed. The Democrats have opportunities, in Congress and also in newly-won state capitals, to show voters they understand that only democracy will be responsive on the economic front. Affordability may rank first, but addressing it depends on the quality of democratic institutions. Americans have given the Democrats the chance to show why that is true. They must not squander it. Democratic victories bring historic breakthroughs for women and minorities. Voters across the US elected a historic slate of women, candidates of colour and other underrepresented politicians on Tuesday, reshaping the face of political leadership as Democrats rode a wave of dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump’s administration ​to major gains nationwide. Democrats flipped control of both the House of Representatives and Senate while winning key statewide races, delivering a series of milestone victories. Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina elected ‌governor of Texas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan the first Muslim elected to the US Senate and Deb Haaland of New Mexico the first Native American woman elected governor. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of a US state, while Xavier Becerra was the first Latino elected as governor of California. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire made history as the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate. The breakthroughs marked a striking expansion of who holds political power ​at the highest levels of American government, in a country where people of marginalised backgrounds have long been underrepresented. “From coast to coast, voters … spoke with clarity. Democrats must now govern courageously,” former Georgia ​gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams said in a statement. Pollsters and political analysts said the Democratic gains appeared to stem from a combination of economic frustration and dissatisfaction with ⁠the Iran war, tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement, perceived government corruption and the country’s broader direction, among other issues. Democrats made unexpected gains in deeply conservative states, suggesting the party attracted Republicans while rebuilding support within its ​traditional coalition, analysts, civil rights leaders and grassroots voter organisations said. Black and Latino voters had become increasingly contested constituencies in recent election cycles. “You can’t take for granted the Hispanic voters in this country, the Black voters ​in this country, the young voters in this country, and if we don’t deliver, they can swing right back,” said Democratic strategist Bakari Sellers. Democratic victories in Republican-leaning states helped flip the House and Senate and signalled a broader voter backlash against Republican leadership, said Vanderbilt University political scientist John Geer, who studies public opinion. “It’s an old-fashioned thumping that we haven’t seen in quite a while,” Geer said. Republicans made a series of promises in 2024, “and almost none of them were kept. This is the ​public’s reaction to it.” Economic concerns, including the rising costs of housing, healthcare, food and fuel, cut across racial and political lines, said Greg Lewis, executive director of Souls to the Polls, a Milwaukee-based civic engagement organisation. Lewis, ​who voted for Wisconsin Democrat David Crowley, the state’s first Black governor-elect, said voters were frustrated with the economic pressures facing their families. “When you start getting into people’s pockets, you have a problem,” Lewis said. In Texas, Hinojosa’s defeat of Governor ‌Greg Abbott ⁠ended a 31-year Republican hold on the governor’s office. Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the US Senate race, delivering one of the night’s biggest surprises in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Democrat Jon Rosenthal won a seat on the Railroad Commission of Texas, becoming the first Jewish candidate elected to statewide executive office, according to the Jewish Herald-Voice. “We all had hope, but to see it come to fruition is breathtaking,” said Joshua Arce, a Texas resident and president of Partnership With Native Americans. He said the results reflected a Republican Party that had failed to offer voters a compelling policy agenda. The election’s gains in representation were not ​limited to Democrats. In Florida, US Representative Byron Donalds, ​a Republican, became the first Black governor elected ⁠in the state’s history. Melik Abdul, a Republican strategist and Trump supporter, said the result underscored tensions between the party’s criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and the growing prominence of Black Republicans. “Republicans spent the last year linking DEI to Black people and the idea that they were unqualified. How ironic that a Black guy ​ends up being the biggest win that Republicans had,” Abdul said. From representation to influence But experts cautioned that electoral breakthroughs do not automatically translate into greater political ​influence, lasting policy changes or ⁠institutional reform. The ability of newly elected officials to shape legislation, control congressional committee agendas, direct government spending and influence party leadership will depend on the institutions they enter, the coalitions they build and the balance of power within their parties, political experts said. Within the Congressional Black Caucus and the Democratic Party more broadly, an influx of new lawmakers could expose generational tensions between established members who hold influential leadership and committee positions and younger lawmakers seeking a greater ⁠role in shaping ​the party’s agenda, said Nadia Brown, director of women’s and gender studies at Georgetown University. “What I think is going to happen, ​what we’ve seen is, unfortunately, that the older members and those in leadership will cannibalise their young, and that’s what I’m really concerned about,” Brown said. Brown said longstanding barriers facing many communities, especially unemployment for Black women, are unlikely to disappear simply because more ​women and people of colour won office. “What was broken by a stroke of a pen cannot be fixed with another, and so it’s going to take time to rebuild,” Brown said.

Australia's Khawaja claims entire team knew about 'Sandpapergate'. Usman Khawaja claimed on Saturday that the entire Australian team knew about the 2018 “Sandpapergate” scandal in Cape Town and said they also employed the tactic during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth. Captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were sent home in disgrace and found by a Cricket Australia investigation to be the only three players with prior knowledge of the ball-tampering plot. Smith was banned for a year and sacked as skipper, Warner was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles, while Bancroft was slapped with a nine-month ban. But former opener Khawaja, who retired this year after 88 Tests, told the Sydney Morning Herald that everyone knew. “It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” he said ahead of the release of his autobiography next week where a chapter is dedicated to the issue. Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it. Khawaja said he spoke in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test urging the team to take collective responsibility, rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft. “In an ideal world, I don’t want to do this,” Khawaja said. “I don’t want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now. “Maybe I thought Davey (Warner) would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn’t think it was going to come down to this.” Darren Lehmann, who was head coach at the time, denied there was widespread knowledge of the plot, while claiming ball-tampering was once ever-present in international cricket. “I don’t think everybody would have known,” he told national broadcaster ABC. “I can’t speak for them (the players) at all. I only know what I know, and I know that ball-tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. “Now it’s obsolete, but that doesn’t make it right either and we paid a heavy price for that.” Comfortable Lehmann, who quit after the series, said Khawaja’s claims dredged up “bad memories” for him, the players and their families. “For the families and the people involved, I feel for them right now because it’s taking them back to a really bad place,” he said. “It’s been eight years. You get to a place where you move on, and I’ve moved on with my life.” In the book, according to the newspaper, Khawaja recounts that discussions about ways to rough up the ball were first held in the dressing room during the second Test at Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha. It culminated in the discovery that sandpaper was effective, and at this point Smith allegedly walked away, saying he did not want to know about it. Bancroft then allegedly volunteered to use sandpaper in South Africa’s first innings in Gqeberha, where the ball swung significantly. Cricket Australia said in a statement it was “comfortable” with the findings of its original investigation, but remained open to new evidence. “There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month’s series in South Africa,” it said. “During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. “All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process. “

France braces for protests as Yellow Vests urge ‘mass disobedience’. French unions and student groups are set to take to the streets for another day of protests on Saturday, while the Yellow Vests movement plans a separate rally in central Paris despite a ban by authorities. The demonstrations follow weeks of youth-led unrest and nationwide strikes that drew hundreds of thousands of workers protesting over the rising cost of living. They come less than six months before voters elect a new head of state to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in the opinion polls. Student groups and trade unions have called for an authorised march in central Paris “against the high cost of living and in support of young people”. Yellow Vests activists, however, have refused to join, instead calling for a separate rally at Place de la Concorde, near the lower house of parliament and presidential palace, despite a ban by authorities. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country. “If there are any rioters or looters… we’ll be ready and waiting for them,” he said. The demonstrations have been largely peaceful, but there have at times been clashes with police or vandalism on their sidelines, including on October 17, when France saw its worst rioting in years. On Thursday, hundreds of thousands of striking workers took to the streets across France in mostly orderly protests, although clashes between demonstrators and police broke out in several cities. ‘Mass disobedience’ The Yellow Vests movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, has called for its banned rally to go ahead. “We are calling for mass disobedience,” said Benjamin Ball, a member of its coordinating committee. Authorities are determined to prevent a repeat of the rioting and looting that marred the Oct 17 demonstrations, although the interior ministry said Thursday’s protests had “generally gone well” despite 642 arrests. The police response has faced criticism for being heavy-handed, with dozens of internal investigations launched into allegations of brutality against demonstrators. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said he will discuss wages and purchasing power with representatives of trade unions and employers’ organisations on Monday. “The only thing that will bring the protests to an end is a response to the demands that have been put forward for several weeks by workers, civil servants, young people and pensioners,” an inter-union coalition said on Friday. The unions are calling for an increase in the minimum wage, which has not received any discretionary boost since 2012, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people. With the European Union’s second-largest economy under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters.

Bushra Bibi approaches IHC over worsening eyesight, seeks treatment from doctors of her choice. ISLAMABAD: Bushra Bibi, wife of former prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan, has approached the Islamabad High Court (IHC), seeking an immediate medical examination by an ophthalmologist and permission to receive treatment from doctors of her choice at her own expense amid concerns over her deteriorating eyesight. Bushra Bibi is serving a seven-year sentence in the £190 million corruption case. In December 2025, she was sen­tenced to 17 years’ imprisonment in the Tosha­khana-2 case, which revolved around the purchase of an expensive jewellery set gifted to Imran by the Saudi crown prince during his May 2021 visit. A miscellaneous application has been filed in the IHC in connection with the pending appeals in the £190 million case , seeking a fresh and comprehensive medical report from Adiala jail authorities regarding her health condition. The application seeks complete details of her diagnosis and treatment and requests the court to direct the jail authorities to produce all relevant medical records. It also asks the court to order an immediate examination by an ophthalmologist, allow her to receive treatment from her personal doctors at her own expense and ensure the provision of appropriate medical facilities. Meanwhile, Barrister Salman Safdar, counsel for the PTI founder, has submitted an affidavit before the IHC detailing his recent meeting with Imran and Bushra at Adiala jail and raising serious concerns about her eyesight. According to the affidavit, jail authorities informed him on October 31 that a meeting with the PTI founder and Bushra had been scheduled for November 2 at 3:30pm. The meeting began at 4pm and lasted approximately 40 minutes. Barrister Safdar stated that Bushra Bibi was wearing exceptionally dark-tinted glasses during the meeting. However, when she removed them at the request of Imran and the counsel, her condition appeared extremely distressing. He said Bushra Bibi told him that she could not tolerate either sunlight or artificial light and was unable to open her eyes without protective glasses. Her eyesight appeared to have deteriorated considerably, giving the impression that her vision had been severely impaired. The affidavit further stated that the PTI founder also appeared visibly concerned about his wife’s deteriorating eyesight. According to the former first lady, doctors who examined her had diagnosed her condition as a “mature cataract” and advised that another eye surgery would be required around November 15. Her first eye surgery was on April 18, after which she was sent back to Adiala jail. She also expressed dissatisfaction with the hygiene standards inside the prison and the medical treatment being provided to her. Barrister Safdar stated that Bushra had specifically requested that her medical examination and treatment be conducted by her personal doctors. He assured her that he would raise the matter before the court. The application urges the IHC to intervene to ensure that Bushra receives immediate specialist medical attention and that her deteriorating eyesight is not further compromised due to any delay in treatment.

LPG availability, fair pricing among govt priorities, says petroleum minister. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said on Saturday that addressing public concerns over the availability and unfair pricing of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was a government priority. Earlier this week, the government unveiled a new LPG policy , aimed at creating competition and supplies through procurement by four state-owned enterprises (SOEs) under government-to-government (G2G) and business-to-business (B2B) arrangements. The government directed four state-owned enterprises to re-enter the LPG import business to ease severe supply constraints and soaring prices. Under the policy, the locally produced gas will be sold through open auctions, which should cut out the intermediaries who profit from the existing arrangement. According to state-run Radio Pakistan , the minister attended the first meeting of the committee formed to ensure transparent auction of LPG. He said the new auction system would help ensure fair distribution of LPG, stability in the supply chain and energy security. Under the new mechanism, local LPG producers would allocate 10 per cent of their production to government-owned marketing companies to meet the needs of remote areas. The remaining 90pc of locally produced LPG would be sold through a transparent auction in the presence of the media. The committee also decided that each company would be allowed to acquire a maximum of 20 metric tonnes of LPG per day through the auction. Daily LPG production would also be monitored, with the data presented to the prime minister. Malik said all eligible companies would be given equal opportunities to participate in the auction, Radio Pakistan reported. LPG, long considered the poor man’s fuel, is now what many middle-class families use for cooking and heating. An increasing number of homes end up buying cylinders as temperatures fall. Earlier this week, Malik assured the public that the government will make utmost efforts to meet the demand for LPG during the winter months. His remarks come as LPG supply has been disrupted due to the closure of Iranian border crossings, resulting in gas cylinders being sold at twice the official rate in the open market. LPG is widely used for rickshaws, but also for cooking and other purposes by those not on the piped gas network. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad, Malik said, “Seeing people’s distress and also knowing that from December and January, winter will be at its peak […] even if the most expensive fuel has to be purchased for the piped network, we will bring it in and try to meet demand through LNG (liquefied natural gas).” The minister assured the public that the government will make “utmost efforts” to ensure piped supply of domestic gas for meal times. Besides this, LPG will be needed for other needs and by those without piped connections, he noted.

PCB adds Aamir Jamal, three uncapped players to Pakistan squad for Sri Lanka Tests. The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Saturday added pace-bowling all-rounder Aamir Jamal and three uncapped players to the Test squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka , taking the strength of the team to 16. Batter Mohammad Tayyab Arif, fast bowlers Ali Shabbir and Saqib Khan have earned their maiden call-ups following impressive performances in domestic cricket and the PCB Patron’s XI’s three-day practice match against Sri Lanka at the Islamabad Club from November 4 to 6. The PCB also released Ali Usman and Abdullah Fazal from the original 14-member squad. The first Test is scheduled to begin at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Monday, with the second to be played at Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium from November 17 to 21. Both matches are part of the ICC World Test Championship 2025-27 cycle, in which Pakistan currently occupy the bottom position, while Sri Lanka are seventh. Aamir, who has represented Pakistan in nine Tests, three ODIs and six T20Is, returns to the squad on the back of strong domestic performances. He was named player of the final in the President’s Trophy Grade-I after taking seven for 32 and scoring 55 to help Markhor IT Solutions win the title. He also made an impact in the opening round of the Quaid-i-Azam Trophy Gold, taking three wickets and scoring 74 and 23 while captaining Lahore Whites. Aamir was among the players sent home during Pakistan’s recent tour of England. Tayyab, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the leading performers in domestic first-class cricket this season. The 19-year-old right-handed batter from Sialkot scored 727 runs in seven matches for Kingsmen Academy in the departmental tournament at an average of 66.09, including three centuries in his maiden season. Ali Shabbir, also 19, has taken 22 wickets in eight first-class matches. He claimed three wickets in the practice game against Sri Lanka, with bowling coach Shaun Tait reportedly impressed by the young fast bowler’s pace and rhythm. Saqib Khan was among the standout performers in Karachi Blues’ Quaid-i-Azam Trophy 2025-26 title-winning campaign. He finished with 47 wickets in nine matches at an average of 20.60, including best figures of seven for 34. The latest additions underline the team management’s emphasis on rewarding domestic performances and providing opportunities to emerging players. The original squad already included several relatively inexperienced players, among them Mohammad Taha, Sameer Minhas, Mohammad Suleman and all-rounder Razaullah. Razaullah made an impressive impression on his Test debut against England at Edgbaston earlier this year, taking four wickets before scoring a rapid 81, which included nine sixes. Meanwhile, experienced fast bowler Mohammad Abbas will lead the pace attack as Pakistan seek to make a strong start to their home Test season. Abbas, who has taken more than 110 Test wickets at an average in the low 20s, said he was keen to register a maiden five-wicket haul on home soil, a milestone that has so far eluded him. “I thank Allah that I am in form and will try to continue it. I owe a big performance — a five-wicket haul — in Pakistan, so I will try to get my name on the board here as well,” he said on the sidelines of the team’s practice session at the Islamabad Club. The 36-year-old has enjoyed considerable success overseas, including career-best figures of six for 54 and a match haul of 10 for 95 against Australia in the UAE in 2018. He also claimed five for 57 at Lord’s earlier this year. Abbas attributed his consistency to regular participation in domestic red-ball competitions and English county cricket, saying he managed to get around 20 to 25 days of competitive cricket almost every year. He also welcomed the inclusion of young players in the squad, describing it as an opportunity for them to establish themselves at the highest level. “This team has quite a few youngsters. The cricket board and management have decided that youngsters should be given a chance. It is a big opportunity for them to show their skills and secure their place for the future. This is a good sign,” he said. Abbas singled out Razaullah as a promising prospect, praising his willingness to learn and improve. The veteran pacer said preparations for the series had gone well, with players getting match practice ahead of the opening Test. He cautioned, however, against taking Sri Lanka lightly, stressing the importance of assessing conditions and performing consistently. Pakistani astronaut to join Shenzhou-24 mission to China's space station. A Pakistani astronaut will travel to China’s Tiangong space station aboard the Shenzhou-24 mission, becoming the first foreigner to visit the orbiting outpost, Beijing’s manned space agency said on Saturday. Pakistan and China are close diplomatic and strategic partners, and signed a deal in February 2025 setting up a Chinese government training programme for Pakistani astronauts. The statement by the China National Space Administration (CNSA) did not give a date of departure, but the mission is expected to take place by the end of the year. However, earlier in October, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the space mission would take place on Nov 25 while addressing a ceremony. The Pakistani astronaut, a payload specialist, will join a short orbital flight before returning with the Shenzhou-23 spaceship, which docked at the Tiangong space station in May, according to the CMSA. The agency did not name the Pakistani crew member, but said in April that astronauts Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud had been chosen to start training in China. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met the two in April, and congratulated them on their selection. He said the space mission was a “matter of pride for the entire nation” and further commended their “round-the-clock efforts” in achieving the milestone. PM Shehbaz hoped that the space mission would “add new dimensions to the brotherly relationship between Pakistan and China”. Beijing has invested heavily in its space programme in recent years — catching up with its main rival the United States — and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030. Pakistan is a natural partner, given the countries decades-long, “all-weather” friendship. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a major foreign investor. In February 2025, Suparco and CMSA had signed a cooperation agreement. Under the pact, two Pakistanis were to train in China, with one joining a mission on the Tiangong space station operated by Beijing. China has been barred from particip­ating in the International Space Station since 2011, when the US prohibited Nasa from collaborating with Chinese space agencies. Since then, Beijing has sought to build partnerships with other countries — including Pakistan — in its expanding space programme.

Supreme Court terms lawyers' vigilance 'foundational' to protecting clients' cases from dismissal. ISLAMABAD: Emphasising the importance of diligent case presentation, the Supreme Court on Saturday reiterated that an advocate’s absolute vigilance was a “foundational requirement” for protecting a client’s case from dismissal in default. This principle is also “reverberated across the world with one voice by dint of a legal maxim ‘ Vigilantibus et non dormientibus jura subveniunt ’, thereby implying that the law assists the vigilant, not those who sleep over their rights”, observed Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar in an eight-page judgment issued on Saturday, which restored two civil revisions that were dismissed for non-prosecution after the petitioner’s counsel could not appear due to Coronavirus infection. A three-member bench, headed by Justice Mazhar and including Justices Musarrat Hilali and Justice Shahid Bilal Hassan, allowed the civil petitions by converting them into appeals and setting aside the Feb 23, 2026 Lahore High Court’s (LHC) rejection of the restoration applications. Last September as well, the SC, while rejecting three civil miscellaneous applications seeking the restoration of review petitions, regretted that litigants and their counsel sometimes treat the court’s benevolence and leniency as a mere procedural formality, disregarding the solemnity of its categorical directives. The present issue arose when the petitioner, Safdar Ali Butt, filed a case before the LHC, but on Feb 2, 2026, both revisions were dismissed for non-prosecution because the petitioner’s counsel, Shahid Azeem Bajwa, could not reach the bench despite being present at the court as he was suffering from Coronavirus. Upon being called, the counsel rushed inside but could not approach the bench due to the crowd in the courtroom. Demonstrating diligence, the petitioner then filed restoration applications the very next day on Feb 3, but these were also dismissed by the LHC on Feb 23, prompting the present appeal to the SC. On Saturday, Justice Mazhar emphasised that, if an advocate lacks a sense of his professional duty, the ultimate sufferer was the client who engaged the advocate on reposing confidence in him. At the same time, Justice Mazhar highlighted that the client should also be vigilant and pursue his case diligently without leaving everything to the lawyer and should not opt to put out of sight or play hide-and-seek tactics based on an advocate’s inattention or negligence. “To ensure effective performance of professional ethics and further to avoid allegations of professional misconduct or violation of canons of practice, the lawyers ought to properly track fixation dates, cause lists and court benches to avoid missing cases due to human error. “They should also make all best possible efforts to handle every facet and dimension of the lis to protect his client’s interests,” the judgement emphasised. The lawyer should also keep his client updated on case progress, risks and even the settlement offers, if any and also avoid conflicts of interest, Justice Mazhar reminded. “In case of overlapping and simultaneous commitments in different courts of law, advocates ought to make alternate arrangements for holding brief even for adjournment requests or must file proper application for adjournment in advance with prior information to the other side’s counsel as a matter of professional ethics,” Justice Mazhar explained. “Sometimes the court dismisses the lawsuit when, despite various opportunities afforded by the court to proceed with the case or producing evidence, the party and his counsel persistently and calculatingly disappear, either due to lack of interest or to drag the proceedings to avoid well-timed disposal on merits,” regretted the judgment. Dismissal in default of a case on the negligence of an advocate without well-grounded sanity is one of the most serious blemishes which disparage and tarnish the professional image and reputation, the judgment highlighted. “Universally, a dismissal due to non-prosecution is considered a plainspoken ineptitude of the lawyers and also a breach of clients’ trust, which also sets the stage for filing complaints against the lawyers alleging professional misconduct to the Bar Councils under the Legal Practitioners and Bar Councils Act, 1973,” Justice Mazhar emphasised. At the same time, Justice Mazhar also observed that courts cannot turn a blind eye to the well-settled doctrine of restoration of a case, which gives carte blanche to courts to resuscitate the lawsuit dismissed in default if sufficient cause is put on record and the demands of justice so demand. “If the sufficient cause is pleaded through a promptly filed application for restoration within the limitation period and satisfactorily explains the absence on the date of hearing, the eventual consensus of the courts across the board is to lean toward compassion,” Justice Mazhar said. “The all-encompassing philosophy of justice articulates that lawsuits must be decided on merits rather than technical knockouts or due to procedural oversights or inadvertences.” Albeit the benefit of a lenient approach cannot be regarded as absolute, he added. Justice Mazhar emphasised that the “scale of justice neither tilts towards automatic dismissal nor automatic restoration, but it should be with a balanced frame of mind and also subject to the law of limitation to ward off and protect a genuine litigant from suffering due to counsel’s blunders, while delineating a strict dividing line against premeditated recklessness and genuine and honest grounds pleaded for restoration of the case to its original position”. He observed that force majeure circumstances or unexpected situations, including physical incapacitation or medical emergencies, are ordinarily acknowledged as convincing grounds to exercise inherent or discretionary powers by courts for restoring cases to “meet the ends of justice with or without imposing costs”. This was because the “indispensable purpose of a court is to determine the actual disputes as an elementary virtue of the administration of civil and criminal justice”. “The rules of procedure are meant to serve justice and not obstruct it,” the judgment concluded.

Pakistan, Sudan sign visa-free travel agreement for official, diplomatic passport holders. Pakistan and Sudan on Saturday signed an agreement on visa-free travel for official and diplomatic passport holders, according to a statement by the Ministry of Interior. “Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and Sudanese Interior Minister Lt Gen Babiker Samra Mustafa Ali signed the agreement,” the ministry said on the social media platform X. “Under the agreement, holders of Pakistani and Sudanese official and diplomatic passports will be able to enter each other’s countries without a visa,” it stated. “Both interior ministers welcomed the visa-free entry agreement for official and diplomatic passports,” the statement said. “This agreement marks an important milestone in bilateral relations between Pakistan and Sudan,” it added. The statement emphasised that the visa-free facility would further facilitate high-level contacts and exchanges of delegations between Pakistan and Sudan. “New opportunities will emerge to promote official-level ties and mutual cooperation between the two countries.” “The agreement will further strengthen friendly relations and institutional cooperation between Pakistan and Sudan, the Sudanese interior minister was quoted as saying. “Both interior ministers reaffirmed their commitment to further consolidating and strengthening bilateral relations,” the statement added. Earlier on Saturday, both countries also decided to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to enhance cooperation in combating cybercrime, the statement by the interior ministry said. The decision was taken during delegation-level talks between interior ministers of both countries. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also attended the meeting. The Sudanese interior minister said his country wanted to benefit from Pakistan’s expertise and experience in combating cybercrime, the statement said. “The two sides also agreed to expand cooperation in security, internal affairs, police training, institutional cooperation, the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) and other sectors.” “Pakistan is ready to extend all possible cooperation to Sudan in peace-building and reconstruction,” Naqvi was quoted as saying. “Pakistan is also ready to provide professional training to Sudanese police officers,” the interior minister said during the meeting. Briefing the visiting minister, Naqvi said that with Nadra’s cooperation, 36 million citizenship cards, 9 million national identity cards, 18 million birth certificates and 500,000 death certificates had been issued in Sudan. He said Nadra was ready to continue cooperation in the civil registration process. On a query by the Sudanese minister, Naqvi ordered immediate resolution of visa issues faced by married Sudanese women in Pakistan, the statement said. “Sudanese citizens can avail medical facilities in Pakistan and will be provided every possible facility in the health sector,” Naqvi said. “Pakistan is a brotherly country and Sudan attaches great importance to cooperation with it in all fields,” the Sudanese interior minister was quoted as saying. He expressed the desire to promote cooperation in various sectors and thanked Pakistan for its cooperation. A day ago, the Sudanese interior minister held a meeting with Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and discussed avenues to enhance bilateral cooperation between their countries. On Thursday, he also met Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif. In a meeting with the prime minister, he commended Pakistan’s support on international forums regarding efforts to restore peace and security in Sudan.

After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand. Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans’ midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity. Vance argued the case for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote , almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the Republican convention in September. He bypassed Trump’s signature policies, including the Iran war and deportations , as polls showed the president’s sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers. The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint and public safety as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his ‘Make America Great Again’ (MAGA) movement, Vance had emerged as their lead crusader, the people said. The shift offered an early glimpse of how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump. Vance hasn’t said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn’t endorsed him or anyone else. But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump’s coalition while separating himself from his boss’s baggage. Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm defeat and laid out a platform for a Republican rebound. He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel. Trump has called Americans’ affordability concerns a Democratic hoax. He launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election. Vance makes unease at the war public The post, for the first time, put Vance openly on the side of ending the war. Three people familiar with the White House and Vance’s communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance’s post. On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump’s more hardline policies. Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. “I would have done nothing different,” he told reporters on Wednesday. A plume of smoke rises after a US-Israeli strike as loud explosions were heard in the central and eastern parts of the Iranian capital, Tehran on March 3, 2026. — AFP/File Reuters could not determine whether Trump was aware of the post in advance. Donald Trump Jr, the president’s eldest son, endorsed Vance’s remarks on social media, along with some conservative allies. The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan. Using the megaphone of the vice presidency He said Vance’s message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028. “It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump,” Ricci said. “This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate.” Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump’s comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood Vance’s perspective on the election results. US Vice President JD Vance arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally on October 28, 2026 in Kinston, North Carolina, the US. — Reuters Democrats are poised to tie Vance or any Republican nominee to Trump in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls. “There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring, said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist. Vance’s brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed, including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the sexual abuse suffered by the victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, may have swung races away from Republicans. Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. Texas Senator Ted Cruz said Republicans hadn’t done enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centres and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent. Vance’s effort to shape the debate was visible during the closing days of the campaign. In stump speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the White House’s immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name. “I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things,” Vance said at one of his final rallies in North Carolina. “And because I want that for me, I want it for you too.”

No, a strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities can’t cook Pakistan, Afghanistan. A hysterical map on social media has cooked up an image of the blast radius of radioactive fallout if Iran’s nuclear facilities were attacked. It fancies that it shows how radiation would reach Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, parts of Afghanistan, and potentially other areas depending on atmospheric conditions. The map is based on the claim that: ‘Pakistan and Afghanistan would be blanketed by the fallout of radiation if nuclear facilities in Iran are attacked.’ Such a broad conclusion reflects an incomplete understanding of the nature of Iran’s nuclear facilities as well as the geographical and metrological factors that would determine the potential consequences of any military strike. It should, therefore, be approached with caution and supported by a rigorous, evidence-based assessment instead of being presented as an inevitable outcome. In our view, this claim has been presented without real data, supporting facts, calculations, or illustrations of a plausible scenario or a string of scenarios resulting from any such attack of this nature. For it to be credible, certain assumptions would need to be established under two possibilities: an attack on facilities carrying fission fragments and irradiated fuel and, an attack on facilities carrying natural uranium, enriched uranium, heavy water, mining and milling facilities, research reactors etc. Then these two possibilities should be considered with the choice and the nature of the attacks if carried out by the United States and its allies. Let us examine two possible scenarios; in one conventional weapons are used and in the other nuclear weapons are used to attack Iran’s facilities. It has been hit by the US and its above-ground structures have been destroyed. The underground allegedly fissionable material is still unknown in quantity and enrichment capacity . Fordow is an underground uranium enrichment facility near Qum, recognized as an advanced enrichment installation located within a mountain complex. The facility has reportedly been struck repeatedly, however, no definitive confirmation has emerged regarding the American claim that it was destroyed, or that radiation plumes are expanding . The Isfahan Nuclear Complex is a uranium conversion and nuclear fuel fabrication facility. The Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant is a commercial VVER-1000 MW pressurized water reactor. A possible fallout if the attack is not restricted to Pakistan or Afghanistan, but will cover the entire Gulf region, including Saudi Arabia. The consequences would be similar to that of Chernobyl which demonstrated that radioactive fallout with highly variable contamination can be detected more than 1000km away. American bases and its allies can also suffer. The Tehran Research Complex is a 5MW research reactor that uses 20% enriched uranium as fuel. The Khondab Heavy Water Reactor is not a facility carrying fissionable materials. The uranium mining and processing facilities are non-fissionable material facilities in terms of radiation fallouts. Iran also possesses supporting facilities for nuclear research, centrifuge manufacturing, hot cells, and other related activities. But they cannot be considered facilities carrying fissionable materials that can lead to radiation fallouts that could reach Pakistan or Afghanistan. The American and Israeli military attacks in June 2025 affected several major Iranian nuclear facilities. Therefore, the list above should not be interpreted as a confirmation that all these installations are currently operational. These facilities do not present the same radiological hazards as operating nuclear power plants. Nevertheless, an assessment of the consequences of the previous attacks indicates that significant radioactive fallout was not detected beyond the affected facilities. Similarly, an attack on Natanz and Fordow would not necessarily result in significant radiological releases into the wider environment because uranium and enriched uranium, although radioactive, do not contain the substantial inventory of fission products found in irradiated reactor fuel. Significant contamination within a damaged enrichment facility is possible. However, a major radiological release affecting Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, or the UAE should not be considered a reasonable default assumption. The IAEA watchdog has already stated that following the June 2025 attacks, radiation levels outside the affected facilities remained normal. Therefore, claims regarding radiological consequences for neighbouring countries should not be based on unsupported assumptions. The situation would be considerably different in the case of a nuclear power plant operating along the Persian Gulf coast. If such a facility were struck by conventional weapons, the potential consequences could be more serious because it contains substantial quantities of radioactive fission products and irradiated nuclear fuel. Its geographical location, together with prevailing wind patterns, could also contribute to a wider radiological exposure and fallout pattern than would be expected from attacks on inland Iranian facilities, many of which are deeply buried or constructed with protective infrastructure in accordance with the safety requirements applicable to civilian nuclear installations. A severe accident involving damage to the reactor core, loss of cooling, or failure of safety barriers could release radioactive material. However, a projectile striking a nuclear power plant does not automatically mean that sufficient radioactive material will be released into the environment to cause a major radiological accident. The consequences would depend on whether the reactor, its safety systems, cooling systems, and supporting infrastructure were damaged, as well as the extent of that damage. Furthermore, attacks on civilian nuclear power plants raise serious issues under international humanitarian law and applicable international conventions, including the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material and Nuclear Facilities (as amended by the 2005 Amendment), 1977 Additional Protocol to the Geneva Convention etc. Any assessment of such an attack must also take into account whether the nuclear power plant is operational at the time of the strike. The most significant question is what military purpose will the United States gain from attacking a nuclear power plant which has been under the IAEA safeguards for decades and is not reported for any diversion of. nuclear materials from the facility. Other nuclear facilities, including research reactors, fuel fabrication plants, uranium conversion facilities, and radioactive material storage locations, may also present some risk of radiological releases. However, these risks are considerably smaller than those associated with a large operating nuclear power plant in terms of radiation fallouts or contamination zones. The overall assessment of the potential consequences for each facility is as follows: Natanz / Fordow enrichment plants : Low radiological consequences beyond the immediate facility, with no reasonable basis for assuming a significant radiological threat to neighboring countries. Isfahan conversion/fuel facilities : Primarily localized chemical and radiological hazards are expected. Research reactors : Potential radiological consequences that would generally be expected to remain within a limited geographical area, potentially extending a few kilometers from the facility, depending on the nature and severity of the incident. Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant and spent fuel storage: Potentially serious transboundary radiological consequences in the event of a severe accident, although such an outcome is not inevitable and would depend on the nature and extent of the damage. What if you go nuclear? Another scenario sometimes discussed is the possibility of using nuclear weapons against Iran or its nuclear facilities. This remains highly speculative and extremely unlikely. Nuclear weapons have been used in warfare only once, in 1945, when the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Since then, despite numerous international conflicts, severe geopolitical crises, and periods of heightened nuclear tensions, no country has resorted to using nuclear weapons in an armed conflict. This restraint reflects the understanding of not only the devastating humanitarian and environmental consequences of their use but also the far-reaching strategic, political, and international repercussions that would inevitably follow. Most importantly, the use of nuclear weapons would not necessarily translate into a military victory for the United States. On the contrary, it could result in a complete loss of control over the Strait of Hormuz as the region may not approve of such an action. Already the US has achieved successful engagement of its military targets at the very onset of the war. And lastly Bushrer does not qualify as a significant military target. Iran’s demonstrated resilience in maintaining its political and military structures during and after the initial strikes against its leadership and strategic installations indicates that the projection of a decisive military victory cannot be sustained unilaterally. Any eventual political settlement would still require the acceptance of the Iranian leadership, which may not be forthcoming. The use of nuclear weapons against Iran would cross an exceptionally dangerous threshold. It would fundamentally alter the international security environment, undermine the longstanding norm against nuclear weapons use, and potentially trigger unpredictable regional and global consequences. The country responsible could face enormous international condemnation, diplomatic isolation, and potentially severe strategic repercussions. This would be an extremely difficult and potentially self-defeating course of action, particularly when a range of conventional military, diplomatic, economic, and other alternatives remain available. Why would any country deliberately do this when the consequences could extend far beyond the immediate conflict and potentially shape international security for generations to come? In our assessment, the use of nuclear weapons should therefore be treated as an extreme hypothetical scenario rather than a realistic expectation in the context of the current confrontation. It is scientifically inappropriate to assume that damage to Iranian uranium enrichment and nuclear fuel-cycle facilities would necessarily expose neighbouring countries to significant levels of radiation. Serious questions can be raised about American professor, Robert A. Pape’s warning that Pakistan and Afghanistan would inevitably face severe radiological consequences ( watch this influencer’s Urdu commentary ). Such an assessment would require a detailed understanding of the specific facility targeted, its operational status, the radioactive inventory involved, the nature and extent of the damage, and the prevailing meteorological conditions and also the war outcome. Significant transboundary radiological fallout cannot simply be presumed; it would require a credible scientific assessment supported by facility-specific data and atmospheric dispersion modelling. A deep understanding is needed of the war objectives of the United States whether they can be achieved by the use of nuclear weapons. The same is true for Israeli military planners as well, except in this case the Iranian ability to respond would perhaps create a new phase of a war cycle which would not be as controllable as believed. A nuclear war is too serious a business to be left for the arbitrary conclusions where it can affect the future of mankind itself.

Govt announces auto policy with focus on cheaper vehicles, EVs. The federal government on Saturday introduced the new auto policy, with a special focus on cheaper vehicles and electric vehicles (EVs). Information Minister Attaullah Tarar and Adviser to the Prime Minister for Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan announced the policy while addressing a press conference in Islamabad. Speaking to the media, Akhtar said that a lot of work was done in drafting the policy, adding that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had invested a lot of time in this regard. He said that the policy rested on six basic pillars: cheaper vehicles, especially for the middle class and lower middle class; exports; localisation; vehicle safety; promotion of EVs; and transparency. He said that the premier had introduced a tariff policy, the purpose of which was to lower the cost of production and the import bill of raw materials. “You will see that prices of cars will come down … the manufacturing cost of automakers will come down; these were the prime minister’s specific instructions. The prices of all vehicles, except luxury vehicles, will come down,” Akhtar said. He explained that prices would come down gradually as the duties for completely built units (CBUs) and assembly plants would come down each year, eventually leading to competitive tariffs after five years. In a post on X, Tarar said the new policy was developed after consultations with all stakeholders, analysis of technical data, and a review of various global models. “Innovation, value addition, and localisation will be promoted in the local industry to create employment opportunities and enable vehicle exports,” he said. The minister highlighted that encouraging EVs will reduce carbon emissions and the oil import bill, adding that incentives have also been provided for establishing charging stations. He termed the initiative a “significant step toward providing Pakistani citizens with affordable, high-quality, and environmentally friendly transportation”. More to follow

Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them. Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”. The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down. But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last. The full article can be read on the Time website. The Central African Republic (CAR) is grappling with the effects of Sudan’s conflict. Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitaries move about freely in Vakaga, a north-eastern prefecture bordering Sudan, fuelling insecurity there. Bangui’s ties with the United Arab Emirates, the RSF’s main backer, are straining its relations with the Sudanese army. Why does it matter? Instability in north-eastern CAR is strengthening local rebel groups, some of which are taking advantage of the war economy to rebuild their capabilities. Bangui’s partnership with Abu Dhabi exposes CAR to retaliation from the Sudanese army. Together, these developments could jeopardise the country’s security gains. What should be done? CAR should work with its partners to provide better security in the north east, while keeping aid levels constant. The UN should maintain its peacekeeping mission. Bangui should ask Abu Dhabi to stop using CAR territory to supply the paramilitaries while keeping channels open with the RSF to reduce violence. Executive Summary The Central African Republic (CAR) is dealing with dangerous spillover from the civil war ravaging neighbouring Sudan. The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the Sudanese army’s main opponent in that conflict, have nearly free rein in the north-eastern border prefecture of Vakaga, where they are endangering the population. The hostilities in Sudan have also revived a war economy that a number of CAR rebel groups are exploiting to rebuild capabilities that had eroded in the last five years under pressure from government forces. Meanwhile, CAR’s growing ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the RSF’s main outside patron, are testing Bangui’s relations with the Sudanese army and exposing the country to blowback. To prevent instability in the north east from undoing progress in protecting the public, Bangui and its partners should mount a more robust security response and maintain humanitarian aid levels. UN peacekeepers should keep patrolling the area. Finally, CAR should request that the UAE desist from supplying the paramilitaries via its territory while keeping channels of dialogue open with the RSF to reduce violence. The conflict in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023, has forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to flee the country. More than 43,000 people – Sudanese refugees and CAR returnees – have sought safety in CAR. Most of the new arrivals have settled in Vakaga prefecture, which abuts Sudan and Chad. Birao, the regional capital, has seen its population double in three years. The sudden influx has severely strained the capacity of Vakaga, a remote region that is among the poorest in the country, to accommodate newcomers, while making access to water and food increasingly difficult. The closure of many international NGO offices in the area since 2025, following cuts in U.S. aid, along with budget restrictions affecting UN agencies, has further weakened the humanitarian response. Accessible by vehicle only via dirt tracks during the dry season, since the 2000s Vakaga has been a haven for several CAR armed groups, which accuse the central government of neglecting the region. These insurgents later joined the Séléka rebel coalition, which seized power in 2013 and plunged the country into civil war. The 2019 peace deal between Bangui and fourteen armed groups, followed by government offensives from 2021 onward, weakened rebels across the country. Vakaga nevertheless remains home to armed movements that either rejected the peace agreement or emerged after it was signed. Chronically under-funded, the national army lacks the capacity to exert effective control of the region, despite support from its partners, notably MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission in CAR, and Russian mercenaries from the Wagner Group. Taking advantage of the porous border and the weakness of state forces, fighters affiliated with the RSF – which has a stronghold in South Darfur, adjacent to Vakaga – have been crossing regularly into north-eastern CAR since 2023. Over the same period, security in Vakaga has deteriorated sharply, a development that observers on the ground attribute largely to the RSF combatants. Heavily armed and poorly disciplined, these fighters engage in criminal activity, including robbery and kidnapping. They have also taken up occupations such as livestock herding and artisanal gold mining, competing with locals and increasingly settling disputes through violence. In response, Bangui has reinforced its garrison in the area, but it has been unable to stem the RSF’s movement across the border. The Sudanese conflict is ... creating new opportunities for CAR armed groups active in the north east. The Sudanese conflict is also creating new opportunities for CAR armed groups active in the north east. Drawing on their cross-border networks, these groups have hired out their fighters to both warring sides in Sudan, acquired weapons and forged new alliances. This war economy has allowed them to recoup some of the financial and material resources they lost over the past five years, jeopardising CAR’s security gains. A rebel attack on the border town of Am-Dafock on 30 June, which left 30 people dead, underscored the growing threat. Backed by well-equipped Sudanese fighters, the assailants managed to push back government and UN forces and occupy the town for several days before withdrawing. Finally, the war in Sudan has strained CAR’s relations with the Sudanese army. Informal cooperation between Bangui and the RSF aimed at containing violence along the border has caused friction between CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadéra and General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who heads the Sudanese army. Meanwhile, CAR has forged closer ties with the RSF’s main external ally, the UAE. The wealthy Gulf state has shown growing economic interest in CAR since 2023, particularly in the gold and energy sectors. This partnership puts Bangui in a delicate position. The UAE has reached agreements with other neighbours of Sudan, notably Chad, to channel weapons to the RSF through their national territory, though Abu Dhabi denies the existence of such supply networks. According to several sources, a small number of Emirati arms shipments destined for the RSF have passed through CAR, including via Vakaga. Attracted by Emirati funding but wary of reprisals from the Sudanese army, Bangui is trying to strike a balance. There is still time to prevent violence from escalating in Vakaga. With support from partners such as the European Union and UN agencies, the CAR authorities should continue to provide humanitarian assistance, despite limited resources, and launch long-term projects to better connect the north east to the rest of the country. Bangui should also strengthen its security partnerships in the area, notably by reviving cooperation with Chad, another neighbour affected by the war in Sudan. Despite severe budget pressures, MINUSCA should retain a robust presence in the area, even if that means redeploying troops from regions facing fewer security threats. UN member states should also avoid prematurely downsizing the mission when they renew its mandate in November. Finally, CAR should ask the UAE to stop using its territory as a supply corridor while creating conditions for peaceful coexistence with the paramilitaries to reduce violence. To preserve its fragile stability, CAR should reaffirm its neutrality in the Sudanese conflict.
