En 2023, Abou Dhabi avait financé la construction d’un hôpital à Amdjarass, une ville de l’est tchadien située à la frontière avec le Darfour, en même temps qu’il y faisait transiter des armes à destination des FSR. L’hôpital d’Amdjarass a soigné des paramilitaires soudanais blessés au combat. Des diplomates étrangers l’ont régulièrement décrit comme une couverture pour les livraisons d’armes. Le Tchad et les EAU démentent catégoriquement ces accusations. « Dozens of UAE flights head to airstrip UN says supplies arms to Sudan rebels », Reuters, 12 décembre 2024. Depuis 2023, des équipements et des combattants auraient transité par la RCA en direction du Soudan, mais toujours en faible volume et de manière ponctuelle. Certaines livraisons auraient été effectuées par Wagner (voir plus haut) ; d’autres proviendraient des EAU. Des témoins locaux et un officier des FSR à Nyala ont confié à Crisis Group que quelques cargaisons d’armes et de matériel envoyées par les EAU et destinées aux FSR auraient emprunté le territoire centrafricain entre 2024 et début 2026, avant de rejoindre Nyala. 164 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, Vakaga et Nyala (Soudan), janvier-avril 2026. Le volume de ces livraisons reste dérisoire par rapport à celui transitant par d’autres pays frontaliers du Soudan. Pour l’instant, la RCA ne constitue donc pas un corridor logistique majeur, mais elle offre une solution de secours pour les EAU, alors que le Tchad a rencontré à plusieurs reprises des difficultés pour acheminer des armes aux FSR en raison de tensions politiques internes. 165 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, septembre 2026. Le Soudan a menacé à plusieurs reprises de représailles les pays laissant transiter des armes pour le compte des FSR. Si le partenariat avec les EAU s’inscrit dans une politique bien établie de Bangui visant à diversifier ses partenariats internationaux, tant sur le plan sécuritaire qu’économique, il n’est pas sans risques. Le Soudan a menacé à plusieurs reprises de représailles les pays laissant transiter des armes pour le compte des FSR. En mars 2025, un général de l’armée soudanaise a affirmé que les aéroports tchadiens utilisés pour acheminer ces livraisons constituaient des « cibles légitimes ». 166 « Le Soudan menace d’attaquer les aéroports tchadiens », Deutsche Welle, 24 mars 2025. En août, le Tchad a accusé l’armée soudanaise d’avoir effectué un bombardement aérien sur son territoire, à plus de 100 kilomètres de la frontière entre les deux pays. 167 « Tchad : l’armée dénonce une incursion de plus de 100 km sur son territoire depuis le Soudan », Tchad Infos , 22 août 2026. Fulbert Ngodji, « Chad blames Sudan’s army for strikes on convoy », Analyst’s Notebook de Crisis Group, 28 août 2026. La RCA pourrait faire l’objet de menaces ou de représailles similaires si elle devenait à son tour une plateforme logistique importante pour les FSR. Pis, le partenariat avec les EAU ne protège pas pour autant le pays des violences commises par des individus associés aux FSR, comme en témoigne la situation dans la Vakaga, mais aussi au Tchad, qui connait lui aussi de fréquents incidents impliquant des paramilitaires soudanais. 168 « L’est du Tchad happé par la guerre au Soudan », op. cit. Pour Bangui, cependant, les bénéfices politiques et économiques immédiats de la collaboration avec les EAU semblent pour le moment l’emporter sur les risques qu’elle fait peser, à plus long terme, sur la sécurité du pays et sur ses relations avec le Soudan. V. Anticiper les dangers à venir Les répercussions de la guerre au Soudan constituent un défi de taille pour le fragile Etat centrafricain et pourraient remettre en cause les progrès sécuritaires enregistrés depuis l’accord de paix de Khartoum en 2019 et l’offensive des forces étatiques contre les groupes armés rebelles en 2021. Alors que les hostilités entre l’armée soudanaise et les FSR se poursuivent au Soudan, la circulation de combattants liés aux paramilitaires dans la préfecture de la Vakaga risque de s’accentuer, alimentée par les défections et les opportunités de pillage évoquées plus haut. 169 « Dissident RSF commander Savannah arrives in Khartoum », Sudan Tribune , 15 mai 2026 ; « In Sudan, RSF defections embolden SAF », Africa Defense Forum, 23 juin 2026. La RCA offre en outre aux FSR quittant le Soudan un cadre sans doute plus favorable que celui d’autres pays voisins, comme le Tchad, dotés d’un appareil sécuritaire plus robuste. L’intensification des frappes de drones par l’armée soudanaise au Darfour méridional pourrait aussi pousser davantage de miliciens à stationner en RCA, à l’abri des bombardements. 170 « Sudan army drone attack on Darfur kills 35, rights group says », Al Jazeera, 2 août 2026 ; « Strikes hit Sudan cities as army chief defiant after US visa snub », Arab News, 27 septembre 2026. Un surcroit d’éléments soudanais dans le nord-est de la RCA pourrait entrainer une nouvelle hausse de la criminalité, des entraves à la circulation des biens et des personnes, une militarisation des litiges socioéconomiques et des violences xénophobes contre les réfugiés soudanais. Cette instabilité pourrait aider les groupes armés centrafricains actifs dans le nord-est à restaurer leurs capacités financières et matérielles. Le FPRC et le PRNC – le premier n’ayant pas réintégré l’accord de 2019 et le second ayant été créé après sa signature – pourraient notamment profiter des rentes offertes par le conflit soudanais pour accroitre leurs recrutements. Des responsables du MPC, comme Algoni Tidjani, ont déjà rejoint la zone des trois frontières (entre le Tchad, le Soudan et la RCA) avec leurs hommes et participé, fin juin, à l’attaque contre Am-Dafock. 171 Entretiens téléphoniques de Crisis Group, représentants de groupes armés, avril 2026. S’ils continuent à se renforcer, les rebelles pourraient mener des attaques dans la Vakaga, occuper des villes ou des axes routiers et chercher à s’étendre aux préfectures limitrophes. Cette dynamique leur donnerait davantage de poids dans les négociations avec le gouvernement en vue d’obtenir des postes et des avantages contre un retour dans l’accord de paix. Des chefs rebelles de l’ASP, comme Arda Hakouma ou Abdoulaye Tago, ont même récemment affirmé que leur objectif final était la prise de Bangui, bien que ces menaces semblent, à ce stade, peu réalistes. 172 Messages écrits et vocaux d’Arda Hakouma et d’Abdoulaye Tago, juillet 2026. Consultés par Crisis Group. Plus les autorités de Bangui tarderont à répondre aux effets déstabilisateurs du conflit soudanais, plus le coût humanitaire, sécuritaire et politique sera élevé pour le pays et sa population. Pour limiter ces risques, le gouvernement centrafricain et ses partenaires devraient agir sur plusieurs fronts. A. Maintenir la réponse humanitaire et désenclaver la Vakaga Tout d’abord, le gouvernement centrafricain devrait s’efforcer de maintenir la réponse humanitaire à son niveau actuel, à défaut de pouvoir la renforcer. Avec l’appui des agences onusiennes et des ONG internationales actives dans la Vakaga, ainsi que des bailleurs de fonds traditionnels du pays comme l’Union européenne (UE), Bangui devrait développer des initiatives socioéconomiques qui bénéficient autant aux réfugiés qu’aux populations locales vulnérables, en particulier dans le domaine de l’agriculture. 173 Ces partenaires pourraient s’inspirer des solutions déployées à l’est du Tchad, où l’UE a par exemple financé la construction de seuils d’épandage permettant d’étendre les surfaces agricoles disponibles. « Tchad : l’UE et le HCR améliorent la production agricole grâce aux seuils d’épandage à Farchana », Alwihda Info , 17 mars 2025. Au-delà de l’urgence, l’Etat centrafricain aurait intérêt à travailler au désenclavement de la zone. La construction de routes, l’une des priorités du plan national de développement 2024-2028, pourrait faire reculer la pauvreté et l’insécurité alimentaire en facilitant le transport des marchandises et en stimulant le commerce entre la région et le reste du pays. 174 « RCA : le plan national de développement (PND) 2024-2028, un nouveau cadre stratégique pour un avenir durable », PNUD, 17 septembre 2024. Des routes bitumées autoriseraient aussi la circulation pendant la saison des pluies et faciliteraient le travail des forces de défense et de sécurité. Elles leur permettraient de patrouiller et d’effectuer des rotations de troupes dans des délais convenables, ce qui contribuerait à améliorer le moral des soldats. L’UE pourrait soutenir cet effort, en contribuant, par exemple, au financement de l’autoroute entre Sibut et Am-Dafock, évoquée plus haut. B. Consolider le dispositif de sécurité et l’accord de paix Pour endiguer la hausse de la criminalité dans la Vakaga, Bangui devrait poursuivre la coopération informelle avec les FSR afin de sécuriser la frontière soudano-centrafricaine. Cette collaboration, engagée en 2024, offre un canal de discussion utile à l’ensemble des parties pour apaiser les tensions et prévenir une escalade en cas d’incidents. Les autorités centrafricaines devraient s’en tenir à leur décision de ne pas formaliser cette coopération pour ne pas légitimer les paramilitaires soudanais et ne pas détériorer davantage la relation entre Bangui et l’armée soudanaise. Elles devraient aussi continuer de limiter cet arrangement à la seule protection de la frontière, afin de ne pas apparaitre comme un soutien des FSR. En parallèle, Bangui devrait poursuivre ses efforts pour préserver l’accord de paix de 2019, ce dernier constituant toujours le cadre de référence pour un retour à la stabilité en RCA. Il devrait assurer sa mise en œuvre avec les groupes qui l’ont réintégré en 2025, en particulier l’UPC, les 3R et le MPC, tout en maintenant ouvertes les négociations avec ceux qui en sont encore absents, comme le FPRC. Les autorités centrafricaines devraient aussi relancer le dialogue avec le Tchad pour clarifier les récentes incompréhensions autour du désarmement des rebelles et réimpliquer N’Djamena dans l’accord. La Minusca et l’UE, qui appuient les programmes de désarmement et de réinsertion, devraient être associées à ces démarches. L’Etat centrafricain gagnerait à intensifier la coopération sécuritaire avec le Tchad pour permettre davantage d’opérations conjointes dans le nord-est du pays. Plus généralement, l’Etat centrafricain gagnerait à intensifier la coopération sécuritaire avec le Tchad pour permettre davantage d’opérations conjointes dans le nord-est du pays. L’armée centrafricaine continuerait ainsi de bénéficier de l’expérience de son homologue tchadienne, mieux aguerrie et équipée. N’Djamena, qui cherche à prévenir les mouvements d’armes et de combattants en provenance du Soudan, bénéficierait autant de ces opérations que la RCA. Enfin, la RCA et ses alliés russes devraient se méfier de l’usage de forces non conventionnelles, comme les « Russes noirs » et les groupes d’autodéfense. Au-delà de l’impunité dont ces miliciens pourraient bénéficier en cas d’exactions contre les civils, leurs opérations risquent de provoquer des réactions violentes des FSR, qui ont déjà attaqué des villages soupçonnés de renseigner les groupes d’autodéfense, et de fragiliser l’accord de paix local d’Am-Dafock. 175 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, Vakaga, avril 2026. De plus, même si ces combattants peuvent aider Bangui à mieux contrôler son territoire, leur allégeance n’est pas garantie à long terme. Ils pourraient aisément se retourner contre les autorités si la rébellion armée leur offrait davantage de perspectives ou si l’Etat centrafricain ne satisfaisait pas leurs demandes, à l’instar des miliciens du groupe Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé, anciens alliés du gouvernement dans le sud-est ayant depuis pris les armes contre Bangui. 176 Voir le rapport Afrique de Crisis Group N°319, Centrafrique, les Zandé tiraillés entre armée, milice et troupes russes , 20 novembre 2025. Si l’Etat ne veut pas se passer de ces forces, il devrait au minimum mieux les encadrer, en sanctionnant les dérapages et les actes de prédation. C. Préserver les opérations de la Minusca La Minusca devrait, autant que possible, maintenir une présence robuste dans le nord-est, en particulier dans la Vakaga. Avec le sud-est, cette région est celle qui enregistre aujourd’hui le plus d’incidents violents liés à des groupes armés en RCA. La mission onusienne devrait continuer de soutenir l’accord de paix d’Am-Dafock, en facilitant les réunions entre ses participants, et étudier la possibilité de reproduire cette formule, qui s’est révélée efficace, si des tensions émergent dans d’autres zones. Elle pourrait aussi renforcer la protection physique des réfugiés – quitte à dégarnir ses forces dans d’autres zones moins exposées aux violences – en augmentant ses patrouilles aux abords des sites d’accueil et en renforçant sa capacité de réaction en cas d’alerte. Parallèlement, elle devrait poursuivre ses efforts en faveur du déploiement de l’autorité de l’Etat dans le nord-est du pays. Les Etats membres de l’ONU, qui doivent renouveler le mandat de la Minusca en novembre, devraient tenir compte de la fragilité de la situation actuelle avant d’envisager une réduction du nombre de Casques bleus dans le pays. 177 Briefing de Crisis Group, Dix défis pour les Nations unies en 2026-2027 , op. cit. Les répercussions de la guerre au Soudan mettent non seulement les civils centrafricains en danger, mais risquent aussi de déstabiliser tout le nord-est de la RCA. La Minusca demeure le seul partenaire extérieur de la RCA mandaté pour protéger les civils contre les violences. Dans les régions reculées, les institutions locales dépendent d’elle pour construire et réhabiliter des bâtiments administratifs, bénéficier d’un soutien logistique et assurer la sécurité de leur personnel. Une réduction trop importante de la présence de la Minusca pourrait créer un vide que les groupes rebelles s’empresseraient de combler, risquant de ramener le pays des années en arrière. 178 « Centrafrique : après les élections, consolider les gains sécuritaires », op. cit. En cas de réduction des effectifs de la Minusca, l’Etat centrafricain pourrait renforcer le dispositif sécuritaire dans le nord-est à l’aide des troupes bilatérales prêtées par le Rwanda. Ces dernières sont pour l’instant déployées autour de Bangui et dans le sud du pays, où la situation sécuritaire est aujourd’hui bien plus stable. Elles pourraient envoyer une force d’intervention rapide, idéalement héliportée, dans le nord-est, afin d’être en mesure de réagir rapidement en cas d’incidents sécuritaires. Cette force pourrait se répartir avec Wagner les zones à sécuriser. D. Poser des limites au partenariat avec les EAU Les EAU devraient éviter d’impliquer la RCA dans leur politique au Soudan afin de préserver la fragile sortie de crise centrafricaine. Une dégradation sécuritaire menacerait les investissements déjà effectués par Abou Dhabi dans le pays et réduirait la capacité des entreprises émiraties à exploiter les opportunités économiques locales. La RCA dispose en effet d’un immense potentiel agricole et minier, tandis que sa position au cœur de l’Afrique pourrait lui permettre de devenir un nœud logistique aérien à l’échelle du continent – autant d’atouts susceptibles de servir la stratégie d’investissements des EAU. 179 Les ressources aurifères de la RCA intéressent les EAU, en particulier l’émirat de Dubaï. Elles pourraient en partie compenser la baisse des exportations d’or soudanais vers Dubaï, lesquelles sont passées de 22,2 tonnes en 2024 à 8,2 tonnes en 2025, selon des statistiques officielles de la Banque centrale du Soudan. « Understanding changing gold exports », Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker, 8 juillet 2026. Les autorités centrafricaines pourraient arguer de leur vulnérabilité particulière vis-à-vis du conflit au Soudan pour dissuader Abou Dhabi d’utiliser le territoire centrafricain pour acheminer des armes aux FSR. Laisser les EAU apporter un soutien aux paramilitaires depuis la RCA expose non seulement le pays à des représailles de l’armée soudanaise, mais ne le protège pas pour autant des violences des FSR dans le nord-est. L’exemple tchadien illustre bien ce risque : les incidents violents impliquant les FSR s’y multiplient, alors même que N’Djamena a autorisé les EAU à approvisionner les FSR depuis son territoire. 180 « L’est du Tchad happé par la guerre au Soudan », op. cit. De plus, à l’inverse du Tchad, la RCA ne dispose pas d’une armée assez forte pour se protéger des débordements du conflit voisin. Les autorités de Bangui pourraient enfin renouer le dialogue avec l’armée soudanaise, en s’appuyant si besoin sur des alliés de Khartoum, tels que l’Arabie Saoudite. De manière générale, diversifier les partenariats afin d’éviter toute situation de dépendance permettrait à la RCA de mieux protéger sa souveraineté. VI. Conclusion Les avancées sécuritaires réalisées par la RCA au cours des dernières années restent fragiles. La guerre au Soudan risque désormais d’inverser cette dynamique en recréant, dans le nord-est du pays, les conditions qui avaient permis aux groupes armés de prospérer au début des années 2010 sous la présidence de François Bozizé : un affaiblissement progressif de l’Etat et un contexte régional propice au renforcement des rebelles. Alors que les combats se poursuivent au Soudan, trois grands dangers guettent la RCA : une circulation accrue de combattants soudanais dans la Vakaga pourrait y aggraver la criminalité et les violences communautaires ; les groupes armés centrafricains pourraient continuer à profiter de l’économie de guerre pour s’enrichir, se réarmer et recruter ; enfin, le rapprochement économique entre la RCA et les EAU, principal parrain des FSR, pourrait exposer le pays à des attaques de l’armée soudanaise. L’histoire récente de la RCA montre que les troubles qui surgissent dans le nord-est n’y restent jamais confinés. Si les tendances actuelles se poursuivent, la région pourrait redevenir un sanctuaire pour les groupes armés et entrainer le pays tout entier dans une nouvelle période d’instabilité. La RCA et ses partenaires disposent toutefois d’une marge de manœuvre pour prévenir ces risques. Malgré les contraintes budgétaires, ils devraient maintenir autant que possible l’aide humanitaire aux réfugiés et investir dans des projets de long terme pour désenclaver la région. Ils devraient aussi y consolider le dispositif de sécurité, y compris en renforçant la coopération militaire entre la RCA et le Tchad et en préservant la présence des Casques bleus, qui jouent un rôle essentiel pour protéger les civils. Les autorités centrafricaines devraient enfin faire preuve de pragmatisme et d’habileté diplomatique. Elles devraient s’adapter aux réalités de la frontière nord, où l’autorité de l’Etat est faible, en poursuivant une collaboration informelle avec les FSR en vue de limiter les déplacements de combattants soudanais en RCA, tout en veillant, malgré l’attrait compréhensible des investissements émiratis, à conserver un statut de neutralité dans le conflit soudanais. Don’t Go Backward on China Policy mloukili Thu, 10/29/2026 - 15:33 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / United States 29 October 2026 1 minutes Don’t Go Backward on China Policy Originally published in Foreign Affairs The Folly of a Hawkish Restoration Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags United States China Nearly halfway through his second term in office, U.S. President Donald Trump has undercut both the United States’ capacity to protect its interests related to China and its role as a provider of regional security in Asia. His undisciplined approach to dealing with Beijing, in which he has focused on building warm personal ties with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and discounted or ignored longstanding sources of tension between the two countries, has reduced Washington’s leverage to shape the relationship. At the same time, Trump’s sustained attacks on allies and partners have driven them to hedge against the United States and strengthen their ties with China. Beijing, in turn, has successfully cast itself as a steady counterweight to an erratic Washington: in 25 of 36 countries that the Pew Research Center surveyed in the spring of 2026—among them Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and Mexico—more respondents had a favorable view of China than of the United States. Given the failures of Trump’s second-term strategy, many Democrats and even moderate Republicans may try to strike more hawkish postures on China after the midterm elections and during the 2028 presidential campaign. This temptation is understandable: there is a strong desire to provide a contrast to a flailing approach and correct what Trump has gotten wrong. But succumbing to it would be dangerous. If Congress and future presidential candidates reflexively adopt a more aggressive stance toward China, they could both undercut a future administration’s capacity to preserve vital diplomatic space with Beijing and further disquiet allies and partners that do not want to be trapped in a new twilight struggle. Overcorrecting Trump’s China policy also would be unlikely to help candidates get elected or boost their public profile in the runup to 2028. Recent polling shows that only a small share of Americans in seven battleground states view China as an enemy or consider it to be one of the top threats to U.S. security. The goal for the next Congress and, eventually, Trump’s successor, should be to prioritize steady competence over performative toughness in dealing with China. Political point scoring and wistful nostalgia for strategies that discount Beijing’s mounting power, and growing domestic support in the United States for great-power calm, would compound Trump’s mistakes rather than mitigate them. A smarter, more coherent China policy—one rooted in disciplined competition with Beijing, patient efforts to build goodwill with anxious allies and partners, and vigorous efforts to refresh the domestic sources of U.S. strength—can make life safer, healthier, and more affordable for Americans. After Serbia’s Election, Foreign Policy Takes a Back Seat, and That’s OK cmoore Thu, 10/29/2026 - 17:58 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Europe 29 October 2026 2 minutes After Serbia’s Election, Foreign Policy Takes a Back Seat, and That’s OK Crisis Group expert Marko Prelec reflects on the foreign policy implications of Serbia’s recent elections Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Serbia Serbia’s election on Sunday 25 October was unprecedented: a non-partisan movement led by university students and their professors toppled an incumbent with a well-oiled patronage machine. The students published a mainly common-sense plan of action heavily focused on cleaning up the state after a decade or more of capture by the outgoing party. Foreign policy statements have, however, made some of Serbia’s neighbours nervous. Start with Kosovo, which Belgrade has long claimed as its own, blocked from UN membership, and sought to manipulate through support for the Kosovo Serb minority. The student movement issued a memorandum in May, calling Kosovo an “inalienable and integral part of the Republic of Serbia” but leavening this by insisting on the need to work “exclusively within the complex currents of the international community”. The plan uses very similar language. The idea that Kosovo is Serbian is a longstanding consensus position in Serbian society, but the students have injected new policy elements that augur well for Kosovo. The movement promises to take apart the patronage machine operating out of the Office for Kosovo and Metohija – ie, the state administration that dispensed hundreds of millions of euros worth of aid to Kosovo Serbs to encourage loyalty to the Serbian List (the only party in Kosovo supported by Belgrade). The List will likely splinter or simply dissolve as a result, leaving Kosovo’s Serbs to organise as they like. The new administration is also unlikely to tolerate figures like Milan Radoičić, who has been indicted for terrorism in Kosovo (he has denied the charges) and is under U.S. sanctions . More broadly, the Vučić regime’s invocation of a “Serbian world” encompassing parts of neighbouring states will likely disappear. The students promise continued support for Serb minorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and Montenegro but without signalling any broader political or territorial agenda. Unlike their predecessors, they do not see the wars of the 1990s as a persistent source of grievance, and have noted that they “should be left to historians”. Serbian politics has been inward focused for years. Vučić made concessions to the EU, for example offering some cooperation on its agenda for Kosovo, and in return Europe overlooked his increasingly authoritarian rule at home. The new government may seek a new bargain, but the new contours of it are not at all clear, and likely won’t be for some time. For now, the students are focused on domestic politics and cleaning house, and Brussels should give them the space to do so, rather than asking them to turn right away to prospects for EU membership. There are some near-term foreign policy priorities – such as maintaining Serbia’s supply of arms and ammunition to Ukraine – which the EU and member states should encourage. Over the longer term, renewing the EU-mediated Kosovo-Serbia dialogue – currently dormant, as neither Vučić nor Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti saw any advantage in compromise – is needed. But Serbia’s friends should give the new government the time and space to develop its own ideas at this promising moment. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/30/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 30 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 30 October 2026 ISRAEL Israelis went to the polls Tuesday for elections in which the majority voted against the incumbent coalition but without producing a clear path to a new government. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc has the largest number of parliamentary seats, at 53, but it is eight short of the 61 needed to govern by itself. Retired general Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc finished second with 48 seats. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the biggest story is the huge turnout among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens, whose parties reached a record nineteen seats in total. The election is over, but the fight for power has just begun. Netanyahu, who will remain caretaker premier for the time being, could seek to form a coalition with elements of Eisenkot’s camp. Or Eisenkot, though he repeatedly pledged not to do so during the campaign, could cobble together a government with one of the Arab lists. A third scenario – neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot forms a large enough coalition, meaning another round of balloting in a few months’ time – may be the most probable. In the meantime, the prime minister has accused Palestinian Arab voters of “stealing the election”, in an effort to undermine the results and stoke anti-Arab prejudice in the Eisenkot bloc’s ranks. SOMALIA The UN is closing its political mission in Somalia, as per a Somali government request made two years ago. For more than three decades, a series of UN missions have used their good offices to help repair relations among various political groups amid persistent civil strife. Mogadishu asked this last one to wind down its work as a sign of the country’s progress toward stability. Despite Somalia’s advancements, the UN is leaving at a delicate time, says Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood. Somalia is in the throes of another political crisis over the timing and format of elections. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud called for a dialogue with opposition factions on these matters in mid-November, but it will take place without UN behind-the-scenes support to help broker compromise. Discord among politicians in Mogadishu, along with dissension between the federal and several regional governments, is a major reason why the authorities struggle to wear down the Al-Shabaab insurgency that holds swathes of the country’s south. VENEZUELA Opposition politician María Corina Machado made a dramatic return to Venezuela Sunday after ten months abroad. The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner got a warm reception as she travelled to Caracas, with tens of thousands cheering as her motorcade passed by. Machado intends to mobilise her supporters to demand an election to replace Delcy Rodríguez, who has been heading an interim government since January, when the U.S. grabbed former President Nicolás Maduro. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says many Venezuelans, whose living conditions continue to deteriorate, would like to see a vote soon. But Machado’s comeback poses a challenge to the slow-paced transition being conducted under U.S. tutelage, especially to the negotiations between the government and an opposition sector led by Dinorah Figuera. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. NIGERIA Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Meanwhile, the increased use of drones against El Obeid could allow for sustained attacks through the now-beginning rainy season, when ground fighting has typically slowed. 26 June 2026 BOLIVIA President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of exception starting Saturday after more than 50 days of protests triggered by a land reform law and planned austerity measures. Authorities say at least 37 people have been injured in clashes between demonstrators and police. The decree bans the protesters’ roadblocks that have paralysed commercial traffic, causing shortages of basic goods in the administrative capital La Paz, and (temporarily) allows the armed forces to assist police in reopening key routes. It does not, however, suspend fundamental rights, as is often the case with states of exception in Latin America. Before making the declaration, Paz had signed an agreement to “pacify” the country with the biggest trade union, the Bolivian Workers’ Central, which withdrew from the streets. COLOMBIA Right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella won Sunday’s presidential runoff by the thinnest margin in Colombian history, defeating Iván Cepeda, who had campaigned on continuing leftist President Gustavo Petro’s social reform agenda. Boasting of his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, who endorsed him before the vote, he has vowed to take an iron-fist approach to organised crime, for instance pledging to bomb narco-traffickers and build mega-prisons. Many Colombians are ready for such measures, says Crisis Group expert Renata Segura, having become frustrated with Petro’s attempts to negotiate “total peace” with criminal and other armed groups. But, as the close vote shows, nearly half the electorate is equally concerned about de la Espriella’s promise to circumvent checks and balances in pursuit of quick fixes. To protect public safety, Colombia needs to balance crimefighting with efforts to plug the gaps in state services that criminal organisations exploit, including for recruitment. The new government should not disregard negotiations, which, if done the right way, have proven an effective tool for reducing violence in Colombia. U.S. - IRAN U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Wednesday that technical delegations from the U.S. and Iran will reconvene at the end of June to resume talks aimed at ending the conflict between the two countries. In this ambitious scope lies promise, but also peril, as a setback on any one front could derail the whole endeavour. 19 June 2026 HAITI Visiting Tuesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Haiti is suffering “the worst humanitarian crisis in the Western Hemisphere”. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says much hope rests on the new force, but whether it can deliver remains to be seen as it builds toward its mandated strength of 5,500. Gangs, meanwhile, appear to be adapting, attacking senior officials and expanding abductions into formerly safe areas, possibly to deter anti-gang operations where kidnapping victims are held. MYANMAR - CHINA Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Myanmar’s coup-leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing on a state visit to Beijing this week. Crisis Group expert Richard Horsey says the state visit’s symbolism may matter more than any individual deal, as it provides Min Aung Hlaing with a measure of the international legitimacy he craves. For China, meanwhile, it is an opportunity to lock in a dependency that provides growing strategic opportunities, while it pushes for greater calm in conflict-affected areas along the Myanmar border. UKRAINE - RUSSIA Overnight into Thursday, Ukraine launched its largest drone assault on Moscow since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, hitting an oil refinery and injuring at least seventeen people. But while such attacks create headlines, they have yet to affect the Kremlin’s warfighting ability and may harden support for the war among the Russian public. 12 June 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Pakistan launched air raids Wednesday across the border with Afghanistan, killing 26 Pakistani Taliban fighters, according to Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. IRAN - U.S. The fragile April ceasefire between Washington and Tehran wobbled as the two sides engaged in increasingly sharp exchanges of fire. U.S. forces launched repeated strikes on Iranian targets as Tehran retaliated by targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait; Iran and Israel also traded blows for the first time in two months. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened that the U.S. would take control of Kharg island, site of Iran’s main oil terminals, and other energy infrastructure. He backtracked later in the day, cancelling new strikes and insisting that a negotiated deal with Tehran was close. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says an agreement would be welcome if it steadies the shaky truce and gives Washington and Tehran a clear path to future negotiations. Those talks are likely to be fraught, however, and may not guarantee the end of hostilities if certain issues remain unresolved, such as Israel’s continued attacks on and occupation of over 20 per cent of Lebanon. WESTERN SAHARA A Moroccan airstrike on Sunday killed three Polisario Front members who were carrying out an attack on Moroccan fortifications in Western Sahara. Among the dead was Lehbib Mohamed Abdelaziz, son of Polisario’s former secretary general, who had been rumoured to be a candidate to become the Front’s leader. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says Petro’s claims raise concerns over a peaceful transfer of power if Cepeda loses, while Trump’s involvement has fuelled resentment over foreign interference, which could further trigger demonstrations. The run-off could also test whether Trump’s endorsement helps or hurts candidates elsewhere in the region. CONFLICT-RELATED SEXUAL VIOLENCE The UN on 29 May released its annual report on conflict-related sexual violence, showing that reported cases more than doubled in 2025 after rising 25 per cent the year before. UN Women also recently reported that in Sudan alone, the number of women and girls needing support after sexual violence has quadrupled since civil war broke out three years ago. Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing says survivor services are increasingly scarce after major U.S. aid cuts in 2025 hit programming for which Washington had been the largest donor. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. Though the policy’s ban on “promoting” abortion exempts cases of rape, many NGOs fear inconsistent enforcement and unclear compliance requirements, leaving them to choose between U.S. conditions that may limit post-rape care and refusing funding at the risk of jeopardising their wider operations. LEBANON Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. Crisis Group expert Max Rodenbeck says the Board’s strategy of making relief for Gaza’s people, whether humanitarian aid or broader hopes for the future, conditional on Hamas’s willingness to surrender its arms is deeply troubling and a recipe for prolonging their misery. KOREAN PENINSULA Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. The same day, Seoul said it had also detected North Korean missile launches toward waters off the peninsula’s western coast. MALI As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). The UN projects that 2.7 million people will cross back into Afghanistan between April and December. Already, nearly 5.9 million refugees have come back since September 2023, many of them forced to do so by harsh Pakistani visa policies amid rising tensions between Islamabad and the Taliban authorities in Kabul. Now the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will likely compel many Afghans living in the Islamic Republic to leave, even as the exodus from Pakistan continues. Many of these people are women, who will face draconian Taliban restrictions on freedom of movement and economic activity. The returnees also include children, some of whom have never even been to Afghanistan and will be at greater risk of child marriage, which the Taliban have lately recognised as a legal act. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says international donors should give generously to fund the $529 million UN response plan, without which many returnees will be destitute. War and violence drove some 32.3 million people from their homes in 2025, the most ever, representing a 60 per cent increase over 2024. The internal displacements in Iran and the Democratic Republic of Congo made up two thirds of the global total. Crisis Group President and CEO Comfort Ero says these numbers are a sobering reminder of how pervasive conflict has become in today’s world. The human cost of war is never abstract. Preventing war means not just saving lives but also sparing people the pain and distress of being uprooted, often with no certainty of ever going home. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says the continued talks are a positive sign. It remains to be seen, however, if Kabul and Islamabad can reach a sustainable settlement that includes verification mechanisms. IRAN The U.S. and Iran agreed Wednesday to a two-week ceasefire in the war that began on 28 February, with negotiations starting Friday in the Pakistani capital. The truce has been honoured in the breach, however, with Israel continuing to bomb Lebanon, Iran hitting Gulf Arab states and commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remaining suppressed. President Donald Trump underscored that the U.S. military is poised to resume hostilities if diplomatic efforts fail. After the fog of war comes the smog of ceasefire, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez. The parties have different interpretations of the ceasefire’s terms and are sticking to maximalist negotiating positions as the high-stakes talks in Islamabad commence. LEBANON On Wednesday, Israel carried out its heaviest airstrikes in Lebanon since its latest war with Hizbollah began on 2 March, killing more than 300 people and injuring over a thousand in just 24 hours. The strikes, which Israel claims aimed to knock out Hizbollah assets, hit densely populated areas in Beirut, the Bekaa valley and southern Lebanon. On Thursday and Friday, Israel launched another 50 air raids, killing at least seventeen more people. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the U.S. and European countries should put concerted pressure on Israel to extend the two-week ceasefire to Lebanon. Since Hizbollah entered the Middle East war, Israeli bombardment has killed more than 1,530 people, including 130 children, and displaced roughly one in every five Lebanese. 3 April 2026 HAITI Fresh gang violence struck central Haiti after the Gran Grif gang attacked Jean-Denis in Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite, a stronghold of community defence groups, on Sunday. Its assaults went on for days, reportedly killing at least 70 people and displacing around 9,000. On Tuesday, Gran Grif reportedly joined another gang, Kokorat San Ras, in seizing parts of nearby Marchand-Dessalines. The flare-up coincides with the arrival of the first Chadian troops under the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, as Kenyan officers who served in the Multinational Security Support mission begin to withdraw. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the attacks show that gangs remain entrenched despite having scaled back their activity in recent months. They control most of the capital Port-au-Prince and are likely assessing their next moves outside it. Haitian security forces must stand ready during the high-risk period ahead. Gangs could go on the offensive as the Kenya-led mission phases out and the new force takes over. IRAN In a speech Wednesday evening, President Donald Trump said the U.S. would hit Iran “extremely hard”, sending it “back to the Stone Age” by bombing power plants if Tehran does not acquiesce to U.S. terms for ending the war. He also claimed such a deal was nearing completion. Washington has meanwhile deployed thousands more troops in the region, while Iran has continued attacks on Israel and Gulf Arab neighbours. Tehran has also kept a stranglehold on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, as Yemen’s Houthis warn that further escalation could prompt them to close the Bab al-Mandab, increasing the strain on maritime traffic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says a month of U.S.-Israeli strikes have brought the Iranian regime no closer to capitulation. So long as Washington and Tehran are pressing maximalist demands, believing they can force the other to yield, the war risks getting worse. SYRIA Sectarian unrest erupted in the predominantly Christian town of Suqaylabiyah in western Syria last Saturday. An argument over allegations of harassment reportedly prompted hundreds of men from the neighbouring Sunni-majority town of Qalaat al-Madiq to rush into Suqaylabiyah, ransacking Christian shops, homes and other property. Clashes lasted for hours until government forces brought in reinforcements to restore order. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the episode underscores persistent shortcomings in Syria's security architecture. State forces tend to react to such incidents rather than help prevent them. Largely drawn from the Sunni majority, these forces lack understanding of minority groups, whose trust in the new authorities is fast eroding. Until the government addresses those weaknesses, the risk of more such violence will remain high – particularly in diverse areas where tensions built over fourteen years of war are still raw. 27 March 2026 IRAN With the Middle East war in its fourth week, the Trump administration submitted to Tehran, via Pakistani mediators, what U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff described as a “fifteen-point action list that forms the framework for a peace deal”. The plan, among other things, would reportedly require that the Islamic Republic give up its capacity to enrich uranium, which it has previously refused to do. Iran has countered with its own list of demands, including that the U.S. withdraw from all its military bases in the Gulf, which Washington has dismissed out of hand. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending more ground troops to the region. A negotiated end to the conflict seems out of reach for now, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as each side thinks its wartime position remains favourable. More likely is a protracted standoff or, worse, a dramatic escalation. IRAQ Fresh hostilities erupted this week between the U.S. and Iraqi militias backed by Tehran. These groups belong to an umbrella institution, the Hashd al-Shaabi, that is formally under the aegis of the Iraqi military commander-in-chief, though some of them operate independently. Those aligned with Iran have launched several rockets at U.S. bases in Iraq and neighbouring countries. A retaliatory U.S. airstrike on the Hashd headquarters in Baghdad killed fifteen fighters and another on a military facility in western Iraq claimed seven more lives. Meanwhile, the peshmerga in Iraqi Kurdistan, who are friendly to Washington, said Iranian missiles hit one of their bases in Erbil, killing six. The Iraqi government protested the infringements upon its sovereignty. But it lacks the leverage to stop the deadly exchanges, says Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel. The country is also facing an impending fiscal crisis, as oil sales have declined steeply with the Strait of Hormuz mostly shut. SUDAN UN agencies issued statements Tuesday protesting a “sharp increase” in drone warfare that is taking a mounting civilian toll. At least 70 people were killed the previous day when drones hit a hospital in East Darfur. Patients, doctors and nurses were among the dead. Another 28 civilians were killed in drone strikes in North Darfur and North Kordofan Thursday. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says both main belligerents in Sudan’s war, the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have stepped up their use of drones in an attempt to get an edge on the battlefield. Meanwhile, the risk of spillover into neighbouring countries is heightening, with the RSF taking a town on the Ethiopian border and fighting continuing on the Chadian frontier. 20 March 2026 CHAD - SUDAN A drone attack Wednesday killed seventeen people in Chad’s border town of Tine, including mourners gathered for a funeral and children playing nearby. The Chadian government accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan of launching the drone. In late February, the RSF had hit Chadian army positions in Tine, killing several Chadian soldiers. President Mahamat Déby ordered a total closure of the border with Sudan, which could have negative humanitarian consequences. The border has officially been closed since April 2023, but until now authorities have been allowing some refugees and aid shipments through. He also warned that Chad would retaliate for any further strikes on its territory, no matter who is responsible. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says Chad, which hosts around one million Sudanese refugees, increasingly risks getting drawn into the war in Sudan as fighting routinely spills across the border. IRAN Oil and gas prices soared and stock markets dived Thursday after Iran struck Qatar’s main natural gas facility, Ras Laffan. The Iranian attack came a day after Israel hit Iran’s South Pars gas field, one of the world’s largest. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these tit-for-tat attacks on hydrocarbon infrastructure signal a new phase in the conflict, now entering its fourth week, as a global energy crisis looms and Gulf Arab states are increasingly caught in the crossfire, with Saudi Arabia warning of military action against Iran as these states’ patience wears thin. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. The attacks mark the second deadliest incident in Maiduguri in the past five years. No group has yet claimed responsibility. The bombings come amid a surge of violence in the country’s north east, with both Boko Haram and the Islamic State-West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate, launching lethal raids. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest attacks indicate that these insurgencies may again be gaining momentum. The Nigerian government and its foreign partners should step up efforts to counter the new challenge and halt rising insecurity in other parts of the country. 13 March 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Drone strikes killed several people Tuesday night in Goma, capital of North Kivu province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including a French woman working with UNICEF and at least two other residents. The M23 rebels who hold the city blamed the Congolese government for the attacks. Kinshasa said an investigation is under way. Despite a formal ceasefire in their conflict, both the Congolese government and the M23 (backed by Rwandan troops) have been acquiring drones as a means of getting around enemy defences. Tuesday’s attacks, along with another in February that killed M23 spokesperson Willy Ngoma, mark a dramatic escalation in the conflict’s aerial warfare. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says Kinshasa, which has purchased Chinese and Turkish drones, is determined to use its new arsenal to show the rebels they are not safe in their bastions. But with civilian casualties mounting, the government’s growing reliance on drones could backfire by costing it international support. Having flexed its muscles, Kinshasa would be well advised to return to the diplomatic arena, pressing for Rwandan withdrawal from the country and returning to negotiations with the M23 with a stronger hand. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The U.S.-Israeli campaign has continued unabated, doing significant damage. Iran has responded with drone and missile strikes in the Gulf and brought traffic in the Strait of Hormuz to a crawl. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. In addition, CrisisWatch monitors over 50 situations (“ standby monitoring ”) to offer timely information if developments indicate a drift toward violence or instability. Entries dating back to 2003 provide easily searchable conflict histories. Building on our global conflict tracker, On the Horizon sounds the alarm about conflicts and crises that may emerge or escalate over the next three to six months in support of global conflict prevention efforts.
